speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday last the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) asked me a question to which I replied at the time. I should like to refer to the question and to my reply. The question was:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour, of which I was not able to give him notice. He may wish to take it as notice. My question is, have any orders in council relating to the payment of the guaranteed annual wage been passed? If so, what is the nature of such orders in council?
The reply I gave was:
The answer is no, Mr. Speaker.
In giving that answer, Mr. Speaker, I understood from the question that my hon. friend was referring to orders in council that may have been passed during the last year or so since the guaranteed annual wage has been very much discussed. In view of the fact that my answer needs amendment, and in view of the discussions on this topic outside the chamber during the last few days, I would ask permission to make a brief statement.
The question of guaranteed annual wage plans is a matter for negotiation between labour and management, and the application of unemployment insurance benefits under any specific contract would have to be judged on the merits of the individual case.
In the newspaper story appearing in the Ottawa Citizen of June 1 reference is made to an order in council passed by the government which, in the words of the article referred to, "has only now come to light", the implication perhaps being that the regulation was suppressed in some way. It would appear that Mr. Swanson, who is widely known in this house as a newspaperman of the highest integrity, has received incomplete or inaccurate information on this matter.
Briefly the facts are these. The regulation in question was passed by order in council not in December of last year but on August 14, 1952. Second, there was no secrecy whatever about the order in council, since it was
published in the Canada Gazette of August 27, 1952 and has since been contained in every edition of the consolidated regulations of the unemployment insurance commission. In addition mention is made of this regulation directly or indirectly in both the employee's handbook and the employer's handbook published by the unemployment insurance commission.
The purpose of the regulation was to enumerate certain types of moneys paid by an employer which would render an employee ineligible for unemployment insurance benefits, such as holiday pay and so on. The reference to the guaranteed annual wage envisaged a situation in which the employer paid full wages to an employee during a period in which he was not actually working. It would obviously be absurd to pay unemployment insurance over and above full pay during a period of idleness.
I might say that this view was fully concurred in by the unemployment insurance advisory committee on July 21, 1952, which was attended by Mr. Percy Bengough representing the Trades and Labour Congress, Mr. S. Wolstein substituting for Mr. George Burt as the representative of the Canadian Congress of Labour, and Mr. Jean Marchand representing the Canadian and Catholic Confederation of Labour.
It should be made clear that all proposed changes in unemployment insurance regulations are discussed fully with representatives of both organized labour and management, and that it is the policy of the government to make no recommendations that will prejudice labour-management negotiations on questions such as the guaranteed annual wage, or on any other matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I table the resolutions to which I referred last evening, and make a short statement about them. These resolutions call for amendments to the Customs Tariff in addition to those amendments proposed in the resolutions which I tabled on the night of the budget. These are not changes in those resolutions but rather further amendments to the Customs Tariff.
The first resolution proposes that the Customs Tariff be amended as of tomorrow

Customs Tariff
to provide for the application of a special additional duty on imports of goods which have been state-subsidized. It is proposed that when goods of a class or kind made or produced in Canada are being subsidized by a government or government agency abroad an additional duty may be levied on imports of such goods equal to the amount of the subsidy.
Many governments are resorting to subsidies of one sort or another to solve certain domestic economic problems, and such subsidized products are entering international trade at an increasing rate. Such subsidized goods, if imported into Canada, might cause or threaten material injury to established Canadian producers. When our legislation was examined it was apparent that there was no clear authority to levy additional duties as a safeguard against the various forms of subsidy and state trading operations with which we might be confronted. The proposed amendment will give authority to levy an additional duty equal to the estimated amount of subsidy.
As hon. members are aware, we and other contracting parties to the general agreement on tariffs and trade have undertaken to limit the use of anti-subsidy duties. I can assure the house that the government intends to apply these duties in conformity with our international obligations.
The second resolution proposes further amendments to schedule A to the Customs Tariff. Members will recall that in my budget speech I stated that it might be necessary to introduce certain tariff changes later if it was decided to renegotiate certain tariff provisions which had been bound under GATT. The resolution proposes certain tariff changes as a result of renegotiation at Geneva. The main commodities involved are canned fruit and ethylene glycol.
It is proposed that canned fruit mixtures containing peaches, pears or apricots be dutiable at the same rates of duty as would be applicable to those fruits if canned separately. This has the effect of raising the duty on the product commonly known as fruit cocktail from 1 cent per pound under the most-favoured-nation tariff to 2 cents per pound. The most-favoured-nation rate on canned peaches is being reduced from cents per pound to 2 cents per pound. There will also be a reduction in the rate of duty on the melons covered by tariff item 95a, from 2 cents each to free.
We also recommend that we implement the report of the tariff board on ethylene -glycol, which I tabled the night of the budget address. It is proposed to establish a rate

of 10 per cent on ethylene glycol and mixtures of ethylene glycol used in antifreeze. Some of these glycol mixtures have been dutiable at 20 per cent and some have been duty free. Along with this adjustment of the rates on ethylene glycol to be used in antifreeze, there will be a reduction of the most-favoured-nation duty from 20 to 15 per cent on the finished antifreeze itself. Ethylene glycol used in explosives will remain duty free.
Our delegation at Geneva negotiated these tariff changes with the delegation of the United States. The rates on canned fruit and ethylene glycol were bound to that country under GATT. Before introducing these tariff changes it was necessary, therefore, to negotiate with the United States. The reduction of the duty on melons, on peaches and on antifreeze are amongst the compensations for the tariff changes on ethylene glycol and canned mixed fruit which we offered to the United States and which they have accepted.
The third of these resolutions proposes that the changes in rates of duty which I have just mentioned should come into force tomorrow.
The fourth resolution proposes that item 1019, which provides for drawback of the duty on bituminous coal for converting into coke for smelting, which was struck out in the budget of 1954, be re-established as of April 7, 1954. This will have the effect of validating coal subventions paid under the Canadian Coal Equality Act of 1930, which, by the terms of that act, depend for their validity upon the existence of item 1019. No change in effective rates of duty on coal is involved, for such coal has been duty free under tariff item 588(d) since the budget of 1952.

Is it
clear that the duty on ethylene glycol, as in the case of those previously mentioned, is the result of negotiations at Geneva, and comes with that sanction?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER THURSDAY, JUNE 9
speechtext: That on and after Monday, June 6, 1955, until the end of the present session, the house shall meet at 11.00 o'clock in the morning of each sitting day, and that in addition to the usual intermission at 6.00 o'clock p.m., there shall also be an intermission every day from 1.00 to 2.30 o'clock p.m.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER THURSDAY, JUNE 9
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER THURSDAY, JUNE 9
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is certainly our wish to facilitate the business of the house in every way this can be done with due regard for the efficient dispatch of public business. I would point out, however, that a number of committees are still sitting, and that they will be sitting in the mornings
Business of the House
next week. If this motion is adopted, it will be a practical impossibility for the members of this house to perform their duties both in the house and on committees in the manner in which public business demands.
This is a situation which should not be accepted by those hon. members who have due regard to the importance of committees. There are certain hon. members who have been suggesting-even within these past few days-that there should be greater vigilance and greater effort on the part of the members of the opposition who sit on the committees. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that there has been as much vigilance as is possible under the restrictions which have been imposed; and most certainly, in some of the committees where it has been possible to examine the facts, excellent work has been done.
I also think it appropriate that I should point out at this time that there has been permitted to be conveyed to the public an impression which is not entirely in keeping with the facts. Comments are made about absenteeism in this house without due regard to the number of committees which have been meeting every day. If it were possible to have a roll call of all members sitting in the house and in committees, at the same time, it would be found that the percentage of members attending to the daily business in this house is much higher than the percentage ordinarily attending to similar business at Westminster at any time.
I mention that fact because I have as high a regard as has any hon. member here for the traditions of the mother of parliaments, the sense of duty displayed there and the dispatch with which public business is transacted. I would remind hon. members here that frequently in a house of some 650 members at Westminster there will be not more than 50 members present dealing with the ordinary debates. That is a much smaller percentage than is ever sitting in this house, because we would not have a quorum if we had as small a percentage as that. I do not say that by way of criticism of Westminster. I say it by way of appropriate explanation of a situation which undoubtedly has been permitted to leave in the minds of many people in Canada an impression which is not consistent with the actual facts of the case.
I think the members of the committees- and I include members on both sides of the house-have been doing their duty in attending those committees. I am not going to introduce in this debate certain comments I might make on other occasions about the way I believe these committees could be operated to better advantage for the dispatch of public

Business of the House
business, but I certainly want to emphasize the fact that those who attend the committees and see what is done there will realize that great effort and preparation are involved.
If we proceed with morning sittings next week while a number of very important committees are still sitting there will then be on the one hand a strain imposed upon members which I do not think is consistent with the good dispatch of business either in the house or in the committees, and on the other hand there will be an impression conveyed by the sparse attendance in the house which will not be consistent with the actual effort being made by the members. There is also the fact that some of the most important business of the year, involving the responsibility of parliament to vote supply in the form of departmental estimates, will not be given the examination it properly should have.
I hope, therefore, the government will consider the points I have put forward and will not seek to commence morning sittings next week, but will postpone them for another week. We are quite ready to take part in morning sittings the moment the major committees have disposed of their business. I do not think it is in the interests of parliament to convey to the public the idea that we are prepared to accept hours which will deny appropriate attention to public business merely in an effort to get out of here by the end of June. If the public business demands that we stay longer, let us stay longer. Let us make sure, however, that we follow a course that is within both the physical and mental capacity of hon. members, having regard to the immense amount of work still before us. Let us also be sure that we do not disregard the impression that would be conveyed by a very sparse attendance while billions of dollars of public funds are being voted.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER THURSDAY, JUNE 9
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER THURSDAY, JUNE 9
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER THURSDAY, JUNE 9
speechtext:
-hon. members are having some fun, and I appreciate it as much as they do. The members of this group have discussed this matter. As far as we are concerned we are prepared to sit here as long as is necessary to complete the business of the house.
I cannot agree with the Leader of the Opposition that because committees are sitting we should delay morning sittings one more week. The fact of the matter is that you will find as many committees have been meeting in the afternoon during the past month as will be meeting in the morning during the next week. I do not believe it would make any difference so far as attendance in the house is concerned.

I should like to join with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) in the observation he made concerning the wrong impression that is created outside because there is not a 100 per cent attendance in this house. From time to time you see some sections of the press carrying headlines about absenteeism in the House of Commons. Many times visitors in the gallery have asked me, as well as other members, why all the members were not in the house. The impression, of course, is created that members are not here.
It should be recalled that during the session some 25 committees are set up in which we can bring together members regardless of party and take hold of the legislation that comes before us, making a pretty well nonpartisan examination of it. Some of the most important work of the house is done through these committees. If you can get a good look at the estimates in these committees you can get an understanding of them.
I am glad the Leader of the Opposition raised the point, because if it were raised by this group it would be said that we were defending absenteeism in industry. Coming from the Leader of the Opposition it is an important observation. We are very glad to join him in trying to clarify that point, at least for the benefit of some sections of the press.
We are quite prepared to support this motion, and if it is necessary to stay here until August the Prime Minister can be assured that we will stay with him. At the same time, we are quite ready to facilitate the work of the house, in conformity with the best examination we can make of the legislation.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER THURSDAY, JUNE 9
speechtext:
Speaking for the group in this corner of the house, Mr. Speaker, I would say that we are ready to stay here and apply ourselves to the business of the country just as long as it is necessary to stay. We would not like to have anyone feel we are unduly rushing government business. But if the government feels it is essential and in the interests of good government, and only good government, to have us sit in the mornings, we are prepared to do that.
I feel, however, that the Leader of the Opposition has brought up a very important point. There are still quite a number of committees meeting in the morning, and certainly attendance in the house in the morning will not be very good if those committees should continue to sit and do their work. On the other hand, as the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) has so well said, there will be just as much absenteeism in the afternoon if the committee meetings

are held then. Consequently I believe we should leave it with the government to decide what they want to do, and we will support them.
There is one comment I should like to make; that is, if the changes in the rules that have been contemplated for some time could have been brought in earlier, I feel satisfied we would not need to start morning sittings next week. However, we are prepared to go along with the government if they feel, in their wisdom, that we should start morning sittings next week.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER THURSDAY, JUNE 9
speechtext:
want to say a word on this motion. I feel the time has come when we should devote extra time to the business of the house. Whether this can best be done by sitting in the morning or extending the sitting in the evening is a matter of opinion. But I believe, sir, you will recall that a year ago we began morning sittings this week and did not conclude the business until June 26.
I recognize that all the Leader of the Opposition has said is correct, and that special care would have to be taken to see that the committee work and the house business were arranged in such a manner that the opposition would be accommodated and able to have their case placed before the public, either in committee or in the house, by those persons they chose for the particular business in hand. I would think we could do that for the one week he has in mind. If, however, hon. members feel that we can lengthen the sessions in the evenings so we can get in extra time next week, the government would of course consider it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

I would have hoped that we could continue next week on the same basis, in view of the committees that are sitting and the necessity of those committees preparing reports. I say that if it is a choice between morning sittings and extending the time in the evenings, I would certainly favour the addition of another hour in the evenings.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER THURSDAY, JUNE 9

I gather, Mr. Speaker, that perhaps I am more accustomed to late hours than some of the hon. members who have interjected. For my own part, and speaking without consultation, I would have thought that an extension for the one week might be better than trying to work out morning sittings and have committees at the same time, because of the fact that they will not
Business of the House
only be holding meetings but will be preparing reports, which in itself is an arduous and responsible task.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER THURSDAY, JUNE 9
speechtext: Well, sir, if we might have permission to make a compromise I would suggest that we might amend the motion to begin morning sittings on Thursday, and try to clear up as much of the committee work as we can in the meantime.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER THURSDAY, JUNE 9
speechtext: No.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Ross Thaicher (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER THURSDAY, JUNE 9
speechtext: I wish the minister would not proceed with this compromise. Many of us who come from western Canada have not been home since Easter. We are getting a little tired. We would like to spend longer hours each day finishing our work and then return to our constituencies. As far as I am concerned, we should be sitting Wednesday nights and Saturdays as well.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER THURSDAY, JUNE 9
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I interject this. I am sick and tired of listening to men from the west insinuate that they are slaves of parliament. Unfortunately, on many occasions members from the east, particularly those from Ontario and Quebec, must go to their constituencies at the request of their constituents. The trip has to be made every week or every second week, back and forth. It takes me 18 hours to go home and 18 hours to come to Ottawa from my constituency. I often envy those gentlemen from the west who sit and loaf over the week ends in Ottawa.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER THURSDAY, JUNE 9
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, after a bit of hilarity may I ask a very solemn question. I suppose this kind of question could only come from a very simple, unsophisticated freshman like myself. I ask it with great deference of the leader of the house. Would it not be possible to have our committee work begin, not at eleven o'clock or 10.30 in the morning, but at nine o'clock?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER THURSDAY, JUNE 9

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER THURSDAY, JUNE 9

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER THURSDAY, JUNE 9
speechtext: We do not want any misunderstanding. The government wishes to arrange the business to the satisfaction of all hon. members so we can expedite it and deal with it properly, and at the same time get out of here at about the time all of us would like to leave. The suggestion I made was a sincere one for the purpose of trying to meet the wishes of those who were not too certain of the attitude they ought to take on this motion. If anyone feels that he would prefer to begin morning sittings on Thursday and will say so, I shall make the motion so hon. members may have a vote as between Thursday morning and Monday morning.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER THURSDAY, JUNE 9
speechtext:
As the mover of the original motion I must say that I am glad to accept the suggested amendment, because I do not think this is a matter upon which the house should divide. There are various views as to what would be the best thing to do in the circumstances, and it is not possible to harmonize the divergent views; but it should be possible to arrive at a compromise that would partly meet the views that have been expressed.
If we could arrive at a solution that would not require any division of the house we would be apt to feel better disposed to cooperate with each other to dispose of the business of the house with all due consideration. We would take as much time as was required to deal with it properly, but I think we would be disposed to leave aside anything that it might not be necessary to have stated at too great length for the proper consideration of the matters we will have before us.
I would think hon. members might want to accept this halfway compromise and have our morning sessions commence on Thursday, to continue to the end of the session. We would count upon each other's good will and desire to be co-operative to bring about in a proper way the disposal of the business of the house perhaps as soon as if we started morning sittings on Monday, after a division of the house that left with any the impression that there was not a genuine desire to go along in a co-operative fashion.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SUGGESTED SUPREME COMMAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence based upon a report in the Montreal Gazette of today, in which it is stated that

the chief of the air staff in a statement made yesterday in Montreal said that the establishment of one supreme command for the defence of North America is inevitable. May I ask if that is a statement of declared government policy?

speakeroldname: Hon. R. O. Campney (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SUGGESTED SUPREME COMMAND
speechtext:
No, that is not a declaration of government policy. I interviewed the chief of the air staff this morning, and I understand that the article in the Gazette to which the Leader of the Opposition has referred is a synopsis of certain extemporaneous remarks the chief of the air staff made while conducting a group of Canadian and United States aviation writers through some of the installations at air defence command headquarters in Montreal. I understand that he was explaining the co-operation and integration which had taken place as between the air services of the two countries.
He assured me that he was careful to point out in his remarks, which as I say were not printed in full, that he was not making a prediction, that he was simply stating a trend in military thinking and that he recognized that it is not government policy to seek the appointment of a supreme commander. In fact his remarks as printed in the Gazette recognized that such a problem is purely a political one.
I may say in relation to this matter that there has been no pressure by our neighbours for such an appointment, and that our relations continue as they were when Secretary of Defence Wilson made a statement, I think it was in January, that we were working closely and harmoniously together and there was no need for any change.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister arising out of the discussion during the last several days as to ministerial responsibility. Constitutionally is a minister in Her Majesty's privy council, or to use the ordinary expression the cabinet, a person employed in the service of Her Majesty?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: I think the ministers, both under our statutes and under the traditions of the constitution, are servants of the sovereign.

speechtext: When we were invited as a special privilege to attend a cabinet meeting at 10 Downing street at the time of the coronation, we received a parchment informing us that the servants of Her Majesty would assemble at 10 Downing street at such and such an hour to deal with Her Majesty's business. Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Income Tax Act and to provide, amongst other things:
1.	That for the 1956 and subsequent taxation years each of the graduated rates of tax at present applicable to individuals be reduced by two percentage points, and that for the 1955 taxation year each of the graduated rates of tax at present applicable to individuals be reduced by one percentage point.
2.	That with respect to income of corporations earned on and after January 1, 1955, the 47 per cent rate of tax on income in excess of $20,000 be reduced to 45 per cent.
3.	That for the 1954 taxation year an individual may deduct from the tax otherwise payable by him the amount of tax on income paid to the government of any province in which he resided, was employed or carried on business, not exceeding 10 per cent of the tax otherwise payable by him.
4.	That for the 1955 and 1956 taxation years an individual who resided, was employed or carried on business in a province in which a tax on income was payable to the government of the province may deduct from the tax otherwise payable by him to Canada that proportion of 10 per cent of his tax otherwise payable that his income for the period during which he resided in the province or his income earned in the province is of his whole income.
5.	That for the 1955 and subsequent taxation years rental income from real property shall not be included in income to which the additional 4 per cent tax on investment income applies.
6.	That the right of an investment company at present to elect as regards its taxable status be repealed and that for the 1955 and subsequent taxation years an investment company be subject to a tax of 20 per cent on its taxable income.
7.	That expenses incurred in the 1955 and subsequent taxation years by a taxpayer in the course of issuing or selling shares of its capital stock or in the course of borrowing money used in the taxpayer's business (other than amounts in respect of commissions, bonus payments or discounts) be allowed as a deduction in computing the income of the taxpayer.
8.	That for the 1955 and subsequent taxation years proceeds of a sale or realization of inventory or accounts receivable of a taxpayer upon or after selling or ceasing to carry on a business be included in computing income, but that the taxpayer be given the option of paying tax in respect thereof at his average rate of tax for the three taxation years immediately preceding the year in which he sold or ceased to carry on the business.

9.	That a corporation resident in Canada that pays a dividend out of its designated surplus to a non-resident corporation or a person exempt from tax, by whom the payer corporation was controlled, be subject to a tax of 15 per cent computed by reference to the amount of the dividend, where control of the payer corporation was acquired after December 31, 1954.
10.	That for the 1956 and subsequent taxation years a corporation more than 10 per cent of whose gross revenue was derived from rents, be disqualified from being treated for tax purposes as a non-resident-owned investment corporation.
11.	That for the 1956 and subsequent taxation years a corporation any part of whose income was derived from leasing or operating ships or aircraft be disqualified from being treated for tax purposes as a foreign business corporation.
12.	That payments made after April 5, 1955, to a non-resident, computed by reference to the amount of timber cut or taken from a timber limit in Canada be subject to the 15 per cent tax on income from Canada of non-residents.
13.	That the exemption of income from metalliferous or industrial mineral mines for the first three years of production be extended to mines coming into production at any time hereafter.
14.	That the special deduction from income allowed for expenses of exploring or drilling for petroleum or natural gas in Canada and the special deduction from income allowed for expenses of searching for minerals in Canada be allowed for expenses incurred at any time hereafter.
15.	That a deduction from income be allowed to a corporation whose principal business is production, refining or marketing of petroleum, petroleum products or natural gas or exploring or drilling for petroleum or natural gas, and to a corporation whose principal business is mining or exploring for minerals, for expenses incurred in the 1954 and subsequent calendar years in exploring or drilling for petroleum or natural gas in Canada or searching for minerals in Canada, if such expenditures were incurred otherwise than on its own account, in consideration for shares or an option or right to purchase shares of a corporation on whose account they were incurred.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few remarks about income tax in general, but first I should like to reiterate to the Minister of Finance the request which has been made year after year for several years, namely that the items in this resolution, of which I think there are fifteen, might be considered separately. We have in these last several years been regarding the whole resolution as one and indivisible, and I am suggesting now that this question might be considered by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have looked over some of the past experiences in this connection, and I am quite prepared to study the problem that has been raised at various times on this very point; but I have not been sufficiently convinced that there ought to be a change in the practice to ask that it be done at this time. Therefore I think we ought to continue considering the resolutions as a whole, and I promise that between now and next year I will have a further look at it to

see if the business of the house could be dealt with more expeditiously by taking them separately.

It could so easily happen- and indeed it has happened-that there might be an item in the resolution which many members wish to vote against, though they would not vote against the whole income tax resolution. That is the reason we ask that these items be dealt with separately. I am not going to press the point further at the moment, but our original request was that we should consider and vote on each item, so that if there was an item on which there was a feeling of opposition, that opposition could be declared in respect of that item and it would not be, so to speak, carried along on the backs of other items which we did not wish to vote against.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the point the hon. member has made, but the same problem confronts him with every resolution that is brought forward in this house. It usually has more than one feature, and he has to accept it as a whole. His point can be met by opposing a particular section of the bill which carries out the resolution to which he is opposed at the moment.

I am not going to press the matter further, but it seems to me that the budget resolutions are quite distinct from the other resolutions-as the minister mentions; here you have definite topics and I should have thought it quite in accordance with the most ordinary method of doing business that we might deal with each one separately and individually. I cannot see that it delays or hampers the carrying on of business. However, I shall not go into it further at the moment.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to make some brief general observations about income tax. I am even going to suggest that there may be such a thing as a spirit of the income tax, though I understand that a learned judge in England said there was no such thing. It is hard to realize how short a time ago it was that the income tax was regarded as practically an intrusion on private life.
It was only a few decades ago that a certain board of trade-I might say, not in the city in which I reside-passed a resolution approving of the principle of the income tax, and aroused a good deal of irritation among the members of the board by so doing. One of my friends, in commenting to me on the resolution, said, "That was a bright idea you had; why didn't you pass a resolution that the telephone was a useful instrument?"
Income Tax Act
But other people were definitely irritated and annoyed. I should like to recall that until a recent date the Income Tax Act used to be called the Income War Tax Act. I forget the date it was changed, but it was quite recent.
If the chairman would allow me to digress from income tax for a moment, I should like to speak on succession duties, and to mention an incident which happened in the city of Toronto, in the days when it certainly was regarded as an intrusion into private life. The following conversation took place when a certain well to do man in Toronto went to see his lawyer and complained about the enormity of the act. He said, "Think of it; when I die, 25 per cent of my estate is going to be torn away from my descendants and given to the university which I hate." In the early days of the succession duty act in Ontario the proceeds from the act went to the University of Toronto. I hope this will not be regarded as a remark made by a jealous graduate of another university. When he asked his lawyer, "What shall I do about it?", the answer was, "Don't die, Smith". That is advice, of course, which we would all like to take.
I should like to refer for a moment to the background of the Income Tax Act. I find it interesting to note that it goes back originally to the French revolution, to 1793, when they had something approximating it. Pitt introduced it in England in 1798 but it was repealed in 1816. Its use in its present form dates from the 1840's, and it was finally settled in England in 1874.
As I say, we have come to regard it as normal here. Anyone who suggested that the income tax was not a normal way of raising revenue would be regarded as mental. I should like to draw attention to the origin of the tax. In 1917 it was introduced by Sir Thomas White. He felt even then, in wartime, that it was necessary to soften up the opposition, which he feared, by commending it as a fair thing that people who had substantial income should be called on to bear a special levy because of the fact other people were risking their lives. He said:
Apart from this necessity, from a financial standpoint, there has arisen. . . . both in this house and in the country, a very natural and, in my view a very just, sentiment that those who are in the enjoyment of substantial incomes should substantially and directly contribute to the growing war expenditures of the dominion.
Then he goes on to say that "the adoption of such a measure is a distinct innovation in federal fiscal legislation". As we all know, the tax was accepted. It has become part of our normal way of carrying on business,

Income Tax Act
and indeed the principle that taxation should be on the basis of capacity to pay is very firm in our minds at the present time. It is taken for granted.
Yet I should like to say a word of caution with regard to the income tax. I deprecate the feeling that exists in certain quarters that the accumulation of wealth is really a bad thing, and that if you can soak the rich people enough, particularly the large corporations, other people will get off very lightly; the idea that in itself it is almost a righteous act, the kind of thing every just man should be prepared to do, to soak these large organizations, to soak anyone who has a large amount of wealth.
Let me say at the outset that I do not think there is anyone in this house more prepared than I am to see the wealthy taxed in just proportion, but I might suggest that there is another aspect of this question which we should not overlook. After all, here is one of our great sources of income, and we should not regard people who are, either in their own right or as heads of corporations, custodians of large volumes of wealth, as people who invite punishment. We should regard them as people whose welfare is of the greatest importance to ourselves.
After all, what does the ordinary man want? The ordinary man wants a job. He wants somebody else to take the risk. He needs someone else who has the initiative. He relies on the energy of somebody else. He is ready and willing to take a job. I have to confess that is true of myself. I would feel a better man if I had organized and sponsored a business of my own. I feel that we tremendously need those men. Indeed, that is what we depend on. I am going to consider in a moment the alternative solution, which of course is the socialist solution, and I am going to dispose of it to my own satisfaction entirely. But at this moment I want to stress the fact-and it is an obvious fact -that most of us want somebody to provide us with a job.
I think the people who do that have every right to be regarded, not as philanthropists, not as benefactors except indirectly, but as people who are performing a most valuable and indeed irreplaceable service to the state. After all, they are the people who take the risks. They are the people who launch out. They are the people who have the energy. They are the people who create the wealth. The rest of us may just as well admit that, for the most part, we are not neck or nothing people. We are people who want security.
I am often disturbed in these days to find how widespread is that feeling, especially among young men who 10 or 15 years ago

were taking the most incredible risks every day of their lives. But now, on coming back to civilian life, they have this desire for security. Whether they feel they have had enough risks to last them for the whole of their lives, I do not know; but it is sometimes disturbing to find how large that desire for security bulks and, conversely, how often we seem to find little of the spirit of enterprise.
I wish here to deal for a moment with the contribution of those who are organized in corporations. There is often a feeling that they get an extremely undue return. I have regretted to hear in this house gross earnings brought forward and used as if that were the return which went to the shareholders of the company. I wish to put on record a few simple figures. These are from a brochure put out by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. I feel quite sure, however, that they have been careful about their figures because it would be a gross error of judgment on their part not to be careful of them. I should like to read a few percentages of the income dollar. These cover some $7 billion of earnings in 1954. The percentages of this income dollar are these: wages and salaries, 22 1 per cent; materials, 46-6 per cent. Then I come down to these figures: depreciation, 3-3 per cent; taxes on income, 41 per cent; dividends, 2-4 per cent and retained in the business, 2-8 per cent.
I want to add the figures of "retained in the business" and "depreciation", making altogether 6-1 per cent. There you see the enormous importance to the rest of us of the success of these businesses, because that amount of money, which is more than twice as much as is paid out in dividends, is retained in the business. That means it goes to sustain and increase, we will hope, employment. Second, I stress the 4-1 per cent figure of taxes on income, which itself is well above the dividends figure. I mention that fact, Mr. Chairman, because when we are dealing with the taxes on these institutions I think it is desirable to remember the great part they play. It is a good thing the taxes have been reduced by the small extent to which that has been done. They are still very heavy, but it has been a step in the right direction.
A moment ago I said I was going to consider the alternative. We must consider the alternative. What is the alternative? The one alternative which I have been describing, and which I submit is what carries us along at the moment, is this. We rely on the energy, initiative and courage of a group in the community who go out and exercise those qualities and make a profit in so doing. I am

not going to suggest that they do not want to make a profit, but I am going to suggest that, in my experience, most of those people are not primarily interested in money. They are primarily interested in success. What does success mean to them? It means creating things. It means making two blades of grass grow where one blade grew before. It means creating better and better articles. It means extending their markets.
I am not going to pretend that these men do not want to make money. Money is, in a way, an imprimatur of success. If they do not make money they will go broke. But my experience is that those people are in there because in this way they find the fullest development of their creative instincts, their energy, their instincts, if you will, of service to the community. I do not want to be sentimental and make any preachment about the matter. To me the most hard-boiled man-the man, if you will, who thinks more about money than he thinks about anything else-nevertheless involuntarily in his success is making the greatest possible contribution to the building up of the country.
Why do I say this? Not because I do not believe these people should pay high taxes. Of course they must pay high taxes. I say it because I think it is important that all of us should try to have a just view of this matter, the government particularly. We have had years of boom during which these high taxes have been levied and paid, and when there have been good profits. I am admitting all that. But on the other hand, as we all know, there is a possible alternative when times are not so good and when taxes automatically become much heavier relatively, even though they remain actually the same.
I want to say a word on the alternative- the only alternative I see-which is that the means of production is not to be owned by individuals but is to be owned by the state. We have seen that system tried. We have seen it tried by people whom we respect, people like ourselves. I am thinking of Britain.
I want to read one or two comments which come from people who, I think, are entitled to be seriously considered. I want to remind the committee of what happened at the labour conference at Margate just a year ago last September, I think it was. I referred to it in this house somewhat more than a year ago. At that conference huge votes were recorded-not one, but several; vote after vote-against further nationalization. I was struck with that fact. There had been every opportunity for nationalization
Income Tax Act
to show what it could do but the votes, I think without exception, at that conference were against nationalization.
I want to read one or two extracts which I have read before and which come from competent and, I hope, detached people commenting on the progress of socialism in Britain. One is from C. E. M. Joad. I am reading from page 405 of a book with an extremely interesting title. It is called "The Conservative Mind". I recommend it to you for study. It is by one Professor Kirk. At page 405 he quotes Joad as saying this:
"Socialism is no longer a creed to conjure with. It is like a hat which has lost its shape because so many wear it; rightly or wrongly, few of us now look to it to revivify our early hopes."
Then Kirk himself goes on to use serious words which I think are worthy of consideration:
Finding that the majority of men seem to lack motive for performing their duties in society, now that the ordinary rewards for ordinary integrity have been abolished or diminished, the socialists are dismayed; they begin to wonder whether their theory of human nature can be at fault.
I read that just for this reason. I believe that in this world in which we live-and I am not speaking of what it will be in 500 years- the number of people who will work without having a personal incentive is not a high proportion of society. I think that is what they have been finding in Britain, and I believe that is the reason the enthusiasm has waned.
I should like to read one other extract which I think it is fair to read, because it comes from a leading socialist and because I think it makes very clear the alternative we face if we pursue the socialist line. My objection to socialism has been twofold, first of all the economic objection, because I never thought it could work, and second and far more serious, I have never believed it could work with freedom.
It is for that reason I wish to read this statement by Mr. Gordon-Walker, former secretary of state for commonwealth relations in the Labour government. He uses very frank, straightforward language which rather shocks me, because it seems to indicate very clearly what a leading socialist regards as the way to progress. Incidentally, I do not believe it is the way of our socialist colleagues in this house. I do not think they would accept this view. My charge against them is that I think they do not face up to the implications of their own theories.
Perhaps there is no harm in interjecting here a little personal story. I do not see how there can be any objection to it. It refers to two men who used to be members of the house. It was told me by the late

Income Tax Act
W. H. Moore, who was a leading Liberal. When he was a member of the house he belonged to a dining club of which J. S. Woodsworth was a member. I wish to say again that I had the greatest respect for Mr. Woodsworth as, indeed, I had for Mr. Moore. Mr. Moore made this remark on one occasion to Mr. Woodsworth. He said, "You have been a very useful member of the house because, although you have not had power, you have had influence, and things have been done in this house that would not have been done if you had not been here". Then he added, "But of course if your party ever came into power you could not be the leader of it any longer". Mr. Woodsworth said, "Why not?" Mr. Moore replied, "If your party came into power it would be a dictatorship, and you are not tough enough to be the leader of a dictatorship. You could not do the kind of things that dictators do".
I only mention that. 1 am sure it is not derogatory to Mr. Woodsworth and it is not intended to be. It came from a man who I think was a real liberal. There are real liberals in the Liberal party; I am not ashamed to confess that. Sometimes I think they are a rather small percentage, but in my view Mr. Moore undoubtedly was a real liberal who by some strange coincidence found himself still in the official Liberal party. Mr. Moore's remarks seemed significant to me, and I am sure they were made in good faith. With this digression, I wish to read now what Gordon-Walker said.
Would the hon. member read a little more loudly?

I shall try to. These are the words of Mr. Gordon-Walker, late secretary of state for commonwealth relations:
The new state will also directly augment authority and social pressure by new powers of punishment and compulsion. So far from withering away, as in theory, both the individualist and the total state should, the new state, if it is to bring into being and serve the better society, must create new offences and punish them.
Another writer whose name is not familiar to me, Mr. E. H. Carr, speaks rather along the same line. He is very candid indeed. He says:
The donkey needs to see the stick as well as the carrot ... I confess that I am less horror-struck than some people at the prospect, which seems to me unavoidable, of an ultimate power of what is called direction of labour resting in some arm of society, whether in an organ of state or of trade unions.
When I read these things, Mr. Chairman, I find myself more than ever obsessed-perhaps it is an obsession-at any rate, more than ever confirmed in my view that whether

or not they intend it the socialist way is the way of dictation and authority, that it cannot be otherwise.
I merely wish to add a word or two. I want to make very clear the reason for these remarks. It is not that I want to weep tears for those who pay income tax. We get a very large percentage of our revenue from it now and it is a fair tax, provided it does not become too heavy. But I do want to answer the view, which I think is held in certain quarters, that there really is almost no limit to what you can take by way of income tax. I want to put in a plea that we look at this thing in a fair way. I believe most businessmen are not working for the money. After all, they cannot eat any more than we do or wear any more clothes than we do, and a great many of them live with great simplicity. But they must have the incentive of being able to make their business a success, and it is with that in mind and in that spirit that I think we should approach this legislation.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to confine my remarks at this time to that portion of the income tax resolutions providing for a reduction in the income tax paid by taxpayers in a province that does not sign a federal-provincial tax agreement. I refer to resolution No. 4, which reads as follows:
That for the 1955 and 1956 taxation years an individual who resided, was employed or carried on business in a province in which a tax on income was payable to the government of the province may deduct from the tax otherwise payable by him to Canada that proportion of 10 per cent of his tax otherwise payable that his income for the period during which he resided in the province or his income earned in the province is of his whole income.
I am afraid this resolution indicates very clearly indeed that the government has turned its back on the original principles it followed at the time of the federal-provincial conferences some ten years ago. The principles announced at that time included full employment, and the principle that in so far as it was possible within the federal jurisdiction, corporation tax and income tax should be the same in all parts of Canada. The proposal to reduce the income tax of taxpayers in a non-agreeing province not only means that the federal government is making a patchwork of its own taxes, but is an open invitation to the wealthier provinces now within the agreement to abandon it.
I have seen figures prepared by tax experts indicating that if the province of Ontario had a 15 per cent income tax on married persons with incomes above $3,000 and on single persons with incomes above $1,500,

the province would in fact gain some $3 million by pulling out of the federal tax agreements. If for no other reason than that this proposal weakens the whole concept of action by the federal government to maintain full employment through fiscal policies I would oppose it, but there are other reasons and other grounds why it should be opposed.
It is rather startling to me that I did not hear any reference by the hon. member for Greenwood, the official financial critic of the Conservative party, to this very important question before us this afternoon. I do not think this proposal squares with what, over the years, we have known to be the rights of the provinces in the field of taxation.
On behalf of the C.C.F. group I want to say that we support resolution No. 3, which provides that in 1954, in a non-tax agreeing province, namely in Quebec, income taxpayers will be allowed to deduct 10 per cent from the amount otherwise paid to the federal government. I believe there is a fundamental and clear difference between allowing a certain percentage of the tax to be deductible and providing, as in resolution No. 4, that taxpayers in certain provinces will pay an income tax rate different than taxpayers in another province.
We in this group support the fundamental right of a province to occupy the field of direct taxation. We know the people of Quebec value that right very highly indeed, just as they value their other rights of language and culture which the C.C.F. party has always supported to the fullest extent. When this problem was being faced by Canadians generally, the Quebec section of the C.C.F. gave a great deal of thought and consideration to it. It is public information that the proposals advanced by the Quebec section of our movement have been adopted by our national movement. Even though the C.C.F. have very little support in Quebec, and on the basis of results in recent elections we have no hope of winning many electoral victories in the near future, we nevertheless adopted a proposition that was eminently fair to all citizens of Canada, and a policy that we believe preserves all of the fundamental rights of Quebec. I suggest those rights are not preserved by resolution No. 4.
This resolution No. 4, I suggest, will provide a personal income tax structure that cannot help but contribute to national disunity. I believe it is inherently wrong; it is inherently unjustifiable for the federal government to set up an income tax structure that will be different in one part of Canada as compared with another part of Canada.
Income Tax Act
I wish at this time to refer to the official position taken by the movement of which I have the honour to be a member at our national council meeting on January 17 of this year. It reads in part as follows:
At a time when farm prices are declining and unemployment increasing, it is essential that a solution to the tax rental dispute be found.
I might say that this was adopted and released before the position of the federal government was made known. It was not, therefore, something that was influenced by any stand taken by the government.
Provided federal responsibility for fiscal policy is maintained, and the financial advantages to the provinces are not reduced, there is no reason why adjustments cannot be made in the present agreements to satisfy Quebec's deep concern over her constitutional rights.
The C.C.F. national council has given careful study to the various alternatives that present themselves and has heard suggestions for improvements in the agreements from several provinces. It believes that a proper solution can be found based on the following principles:
(a)	Every province to have the option of imposing its own income tax with deductibility, up to but not exceeding, the amount it would receive from the federal government under the tax rental agreements.
This proposal, if fully adopted, would not cost the federal treasury any more than it is offering to the provinces that might sign tax rental agreements.
(b)	Should the provincial tax exceed or fall short of this amount in any year the difference should be adjusted, any deficiency to be made up by a federal grant and any excess to be returned to the federal treasury.
In other words, by following such a policy the federal government could implement all the essential fiscal policies necessary to deal with the problem of unemployment, and it would be making it possible for taxpayers in all provinces in Canada to pay the same income taxes. I feel that such a proposal is not only right because it would tend to bring about equality of income tax, but also because it would make it possible for a province to exercise a fundamental right namely to occupy the income tax field and obtain the same amount by imposing its own tax as it would obtain from the federal government under a tax agreement. Such a proposal would not impose any heavier tax burden on the people of that province. The proposal by the Liberal government that we are discussing today, while it appears in a monetary sense to help the taxpayers of Quebec, in fact is an insult to the people of Quebec who value their fundamental rights so highly. It is this proposal to which we are completely and unalterably opposed.
I do not believe this proposal can be justified on any grounds whatever. Would the government consider for one minute, I ask,

Income Tax Act
imposing an excise tax on some particular article at a higher rate in one province or group of provinces than would apply on the article purchased by taxpayers in another province or group of provinces? Would the federal government consider for one moment placing a higher tax on automobiles sold in Ontario than on automobiles sold in Manitoba? It is such a ridiculous proposition. We all know that good Canadians who value national unity would not stand for such a difference in taxation. Yet in the income tax field that is precisely the proposition we have before us, and that is precisely the result that will flow from the adoption of resolution No. 4.
Would the government set a different sales tax, I ask, or any other tax, on electric refrigerators or electric stoves, so that the housewife in Newfoundland would have to pay more because of a higher federal tax on those articles than a housewife in British Columbia? I am sure again this illustration is so ridiculous that no member in this house would publicly support it. Yet-

speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? If that is his view, why has he never opposed having different federal rates in different provinces in relation to the corporation income tax? It has been in effect for 5 or 6 years. Why is it right for corporation taxes and wrong for personal taxes?

The answer to that question is pretty obvious. It is obviously wrong to impose a different tax on persons, and may or may not be wrong on an inanimate object such as a corporation. That question by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration suggests that he is quite happy that the income taxpayers in one province will be paying a tax different from that paid by taxpayers in other provinces. I suggest that is a proposition no member in this house should support.
What value can there possibly be in this resolution? Had the Prime Minister brought in a proposition which gave more to the province of Quebec and to the income taxpayers of that province by allowing full deductibility of the provincial tax up to the maximum amount the province would receive under a dominion-provincial tax agreement, the C.C.F. party would have supported it completely. But this looks like a rather ill-conceived attempt to maintain the political fortunes of the Liberal party in one province. I do not think the people of Quebec, being good, honest Canadians, believing as they do in their fundamental rights, will appreciate this move and support it, any more than will

the taxpayers in any other province of Canada. As I have said, I believe this proposition is wrong in every respect.
The Quebec federation of industrial unions has given a great deal of study to this matter, and has found that the proposal by the government is wrong for four reasons. The first reason they list is that it is unilateral; that it is applied to one province and one province only because, of course, that is the only province that is not under any tax agreement at the present time.
The second reason they give is that it does not square with the cyclical ideas of fiscal agreements; that if this were carried on in a time of deflation, with provinces outside the agreements, a reduction in federal personal income tax could be met by a provincial government occupying the same field, and therefore the increased purchasing power in the hands of the public that the government might hope to provide by such a taxation policy-and that is the government's whole theory, as we have been told so often, of cyclical financing-would be abrogated.
The third reason they suggest as to why this proposal is wrong is that it is an injustice to the province of Quebec. I shall not further elaborate on why it is an injustice; as I think I have already very fully covered that point.
The fourth reason they give for opposing this measure is that it is a hindrance to national unity. When the bill is introduced which provides for the 10 per cent deductibility of income tax as provided in resolution No. 3, the C.C.F. party will give it its full support, but we shall oppose the proposition that the federal government should reduce taxes in any province below the level of income tax in any other provinces.
I hope with all my heart that the coming federal-provincial conference will be successful in every way, that there will be full agreement by all the provinces. I would hope that agreement will be so widespread that a year from now the government will, by action at that time, remove the inequalities and injustices that flow from the implementation of its present proposal. If that should not happen I hope the Prime Minister himself, who I know has given this problem a great deal of attention and consideration, will finally see that it is fundamentally wrong to have different rates of taxation applied by the federal government to taxpayers in different provinces. I hope during the present session he will yet withdraw this proposal and bring in a proposal of deductibility which will do more for the people of Quebec, and at the same time be a contribution to national unity in our country.

I said, Mr. Chairman, that it is not within the jurisdiction of Ottawa to subsidize our universities and even less to raise taxes for that purpose. That is the exclusive privilege of the provinces.
When the central government exceeds its rights, it does an injustice to the Quebec taxpayers who are forced to pay a large share of these grants which go more often than not to institutions who refuse to acknowledge the rights of my compatriots in the other provinces.
Some people wonder why Quebec refuses thus each year the millions offered by the federal government.
The reason is a simple one: we value more our rights than money.
No more than the rest of the citizens of Canada do we enjoy paying taxes. We know however that our survival, as an ethnic entity, is assured as long as we retain control over our educational system.
We are proud of our origin, of our French culture, of our history, of our customs and age-old traditions.
I take pleasure here in quoting an article written by Mr. Murray Ballantyne which has been published in pamphlet form by the Institut Social Populaire of Montreal. Here is what this English-speaking Canadian says about French Canadians:
(Text):
Have you ever wondered what it feels like to be a French-speaking Canadian? First of all they are in their own country. They are the senior Canadians. Long ago they reached that level of national, North American consciousness to which many of us are but now attaining.
In a great arc from the mouth of the St. Lawrence to the mouth of the Mississippi, the French were the first to explore, the first to trade, and the first to evangelize. Kingston, Toronto, Winnipeg, Detroit, Pittsburgh, St. Louis and New Orleans-all stand on sites discovered by French daring and occupied by French genius. It was the French tongue that was first heard here by the Indians, it was the blood of French missionaries that first rendered this soil sacred to French memory.
(Translation):
Further on, this distinguished professor stated, with regard to the situation imposed on our fellow citizens in the other provinces of the dominion, with regard to schools:
(Text):
The B.N.A. Act declares that the Protestants in Quebec shall have in education all the "powers, privileges, and duties" enjoyed by the Catholics in Ontario.
How has this compromise, this gentleman's agreement, been honoured? What do we find today? In Quebec the Protestants have the fullest possible enjoyment of their school rights. Nothing that they could ask has been denied them. But in Ontario, which was to have been the paragon.

Catholic schools can be carried beyond the primary level only at the cost of double taxation. And even at the primary level it is almost impossible for Catholics to enjoy their fair share of corporate taxes. As for the French tongue in that province, it is more than 40 years since regulation 17 forbade that language except as a subject of instruction. The English in Quebec are perfectly free to teach in their own tongue. The French in Ontario are not.
Admittedly what has happened to separate schools in Ontario is at least partly the result of judicial decisions. And admittedly the parliament and courts of Quebec are officially bilingual while those of Ontario are not. Still the French feel that Quebec has kept the original agreement in letter and in spirit, and that Ontario has not.
Out west. Manitoba was established by federal act in 1870 as officially bilingual and with full educational equality for Catholics and Protestants. Today the French tongue has been deprived of all recognition in that province, and Catholics who want their own schools have to pay taxes to the public schools as well. Thus the French-Canadians are once again made familiar with the penalty of double taxation.
In Saskatchewan and Alberta it is much the same story. Catholic schools have not been crippled quite as cruelly in these provinces as in Manitoba, but the French language has been deprived of all status. Sir John A. Macdonald opposed the move to make English the only official language in those parts. Speaking of this proposed suppression in 1890 he said: "I believe that it would be impossible if it were tried, and it would be foolish and wicked if it were possible."
Nevertheless in 1892 the legislative assembly of the then North West Territories carried out this "wicked" act.
New Brunswick is another province in which the minority feels that it has been deprived of its rights.
As for British Columbia, the French cannot claim that earlier rights of language or education have been abolished because so far as I know they never had any rights there. They never had any rights, that is to say, in positive law. But have they not natural rights, and are these natural rights not infringed as they see their children trudge to schools built at their own double expense while other children are driven to public schools in public busses to which the Catholics have had to contribute their full share of the cost?
(Translation):
I wanted to quote this article, Mr. Chairman, to show the position of French Canadians in the other provinces and to show how right we are to keep our money in the province and to levy an income tax, in order to be able to pay to our universities, seminaries and colleges the very same grants, in so far as that is possible, that the federal government wants to foist upon us by unconstitutional methods. I would like the federal government not only to grant us 10 per cent, but a complete deduction of the tax raised by the provincial government.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
It has been moved by the hon. member for Chicoutimi, that paragraph 3 of the Income Tax Act resolution be amended by leaving out all the words after the word "business". The hon. member has read to the committee the resolution as it would then read.
In my opinion it would quite obviously affect the revenue which would be derived by the federal authority if his amendment were to be adopted. Therefore it is my opinion that the amendment is undoubtedly out of order. I have before me some-and I think the committee is familiar with many-decisions holding that it is not competent for a private member to introduce an amendment to a tax resolution which would have the result of-I believe this is the expression -affecting the balance of ways and means. Therefore I feel I have no alternative but to state that the hon. member's amendment is out of order.

Mr. Chairman, I was a little amazed to hear what the hon. member for Assiniboia said about the rights of Quebec. I should like to congratulate him because there has been a great change. Ever since the Prime Minister stated the government were going to permit a 10 per cent deduction he and all the members of his party have said the government were going back on what they had already done. I quote what the hon. member said in January, 1955, at page 345 of Hansard:
The statement by the Prime Minister of Canada in which he said that the Canadian income tax law would be amended to reduce the federal tax by 10 per cent in Quebec means, in my opinion, a complete surrender by the federal government of Canada to Premier Duplessis in Quebec.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, some of the arguments put forth a while ago by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), who said that a double taxation would be levied because the government of the province of Quebec had set a fiscal basis different from that of the other provinces, deserve some consideration.
The hon. member forgets that even though in the province of Quebec some taxpayers will pay less than those of other provinces, it is not through any favour of the federal government, but rather because the province has not levied through its legislation as much as the federal government allows. He cannot credit the federal government with results arising from provincial legislation. It is truly

Income Tax Act
the outcome of the provincial government's generosity. I do not think that he can censure or congratulate the federal government on that score or use this as a pretext to oppose the 10 per cent deduction or say that it is another step towards surrender.
However, that 10 per cent deduction cannot be satisfactory to the province of Quebec, especially since it is not the only aspect to be taken into consideration. We have never mentioned any amount when we have asked for a full deduction. It would be foolish to fight for less money than was offered by way of the fiscal agreements. The essence of the matter lies in a principle and not exclusively on finance. It is the principle of autonomy, the respect of our various forms of government, and that principle forms the basis of Quebec's demands. That is why, even if the 10 per cent deduction means a step towards compromise, it does nothing as far as our rights are concerned, from the point of view of autonomy, even though from the sole political standpoint it may seem that the Prime Minister is not the loser and that the premier of the province is also the winner.
The C.C.F. party, which hides its dictatorial program under a socialist label, sees in fiscal agreements an ideal way of making its dream of centralization come true. That is why it considers that any encroachment upon the fiscal agreements is an attack on our most precious assets. That is why the leader of the party (Mr. Coldwell) so strongly opposed any amendment to the fiscal agreements, in which he was admirably seconded by the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) and by several other of their supporters.
They want to safeguard the fiscal agreements, even if to that end they would have to destroy the constitution, as was so often done by spokesmen for the government who said at the time: "You must take it or leave it, even if you have rights, even if it should ignore the rights of the provinces".
People sometimes are concerned over the fact that the great majority of the people do not take any interest in politics, that people seem to have so little confidence in politicians. When the rights governed by the constitution are dealt with in such an illogical way, such a stand by the electors is not surprising.
How did the fiscal agreements come about? First of all, advantage was taken of the abnormal situation brought about by the war, to borrow the rights of the provinces. After the war, another pretext was needed and a very righteous one was found: it was necessary to ask rich provinces to help the poor provinces.

That all-powerful argument could be assimilated to that of a judge who would say to the crown attorney in a trial for robbery: "Well, that belongs to the plaintiff; he is entitled to it, but it does not matter whether he needs it or not, we have decided to use it to help someone poorer than he is".
In the meantime, it was costing the province of Quebec more than $30 million a year to adhere to that principle. It was undoubtedly thought that the cost would be so heavy that she would not be able to stand it very long and that sooner or later she would have to give up.
Last year, availing herself of her rights, the province of Quebec decided to levy her own income tax. At first the federal government was surprised and somewhat concerned, but on second thought they became reassured and said: Mr. Duplessis fell into the trap; he levied a tax and the federal government will see to it that he bears the onus of double taxation, which is always unpopular. However their satisfaction did not last very long, when they found that all the people of Quebec supported the provincial government and laid upon the federal government, where it should rest, that onus of double taxation.
The federal government found itself in a spot and the argument relating to the poor provinces lost its weight.
Following ultra-nationalist ideas, as they were accused last year of doing, independent members dared to move an amendment during the debate on the budget last year, which asked for the full deduction of the Quebec income tax. The then minister of finance (Mr. Abbott) rejected those too daring claims when he said-and these are his very words: "The federal government keeps the door open and would be ready to co-operate", adding however that no deduction greater than 5 per cent could be granted without straining overly the resources of the treasury.
The argument was not favourably received in the province of Quebec. The Prime Minister also made in the Reform Club a statement which had an extraordinary effect in Quebec. Then they apparently got together and thought of an offer which might be a political face-saving but which would do nothing to safeguard the principle we wished to uphold. With a surplus of over $13 million in 1953-1954, if my memory serves me right, the federal government was not in a position to grant a deduction of over 5 per cent. This year though, with a deficit of $160 million, it can grant one of 10 per cent. That is just another instance of the inconsistencies which are indulged in so as to maintain these fiscal agreements which are contrary to the rights of the provinces.

Income Tax Act
I was listening a moment ago to the hon. member for Assiniboia who said that the deduction proposed was absolutely unjust for the other provinces, since it would mean double taxation for Quebec and that even the people of Quebec, if I heard him correctly, could not claim to be real citizens if they dared claim what other provinces did not have.
I do not wish to repeat the arguments already advanced by my colleague from Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon) but if one thinks of the double taxation for separate school purposes in the other provinces, it is easy to realize how it can hurt. In short, Mr. Chairman, the government was faced with a budgetary problem, in this, that if it were to give more to the province of Quebec and if the province of Ontario requested the same treatment, the federal government would no longer be in a position to fulfil its obligations. However, this argument can no longer be offered today, as, at last, all agree to claim from the federal government, not 5 per cent, nor 10 per cent, but a full deduction, providing, however, that the amount that we claim does not exceed that which is offered under the fiscal agreements. It therefore means that the budget balance is maintained, that neither the treasury argument, nor the argument to the effect that the other provinces allegedly are being wronged, can be advanced.
That is why I support the claims of my colleague for Chicoutimi asking the federal government to reconsider the situation and to allow the province to administer and collect the taxes that it needs to fulfil its obligations as determined by the constitution, provided the amounts offered under the fiscal agreements be not exceeded.
