we seem to have ranged a long way from the budget resolutions on occasion in the last hour or so. We people in British Columbia may be peculiar-I suppose we are-as we are the only province in Canada apparently that maintains one school system. It is a school system that was established nearly 100 years
ago, and it was established on certain principles. One of those principles was that it should not be a divisive influence in our community, that the schools should be secular schools, and that the question of religious instruction should be left entirely to the churches and to the homes. That decision has been maintained for nearly a century. I myself, when I went to school in British Columbia, went to school with a number of Roman Catholics. I was not aware of that fact at the time. It was not until I left school and met them afterwards that I became aware of the fact that those boys and girls with whom I had gone to school had been Roman Catholics.
We in British Columbia feel that one of the purposes of a system of education is to create in the minds of the children a sense of their unity with all other Canadians, not to drive home to them a sense of their difference from other Canadians. It is for that reason that the people of British Columbia have maintained this school system. I may say this. We are not too happy when we have stigmatized as injustice to minorities this decision that has been made and has been maintained by a democratic majority in British Columbia.
Now, Mr. Chairman, we started off this afternoon with, shall I say, an even greater breach of the letter of this discussion when the hon. member for Greenwood was speaking. I am not at all sure that the hon. member for Greenwood and I would be in order to discuss the finer points of the socialist and capitalist theories on the basis of the budget resolutions. I would, however, make this comment. I do wish that the critics of socialism would read books about socialism written by socialists rather than read the second-hand comments of people who obviously have no conception whatever of the fundamental socialist principles.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.

Would it not be fair for me to answer that I did at least cull from this source, of which he does not think so very highly, statements by people who are in the ranks of the sanctified and who are authorized as such to speak the pure word of socialism?

Well, I was just going to say that I knew quite well the hon. member would throw the Hon. Patrick Gordon-Walker at me. Indeed, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Greenwood-

The Depuiy Chairman: Order. Before I allow the hon. member for Nanaimo to complete the sentence which I am now interrupting I think I should point out to the committee that the committee is not dealing with the question of minority rights, language, or education. Partly through my own fault, statements were made in that connection and I permitted them to be answered. I propose now, in so far as that part of the discussion is concerned, to regard it as concluded. The hon. member for Nanaimo considers that he is justified in replying to some remarks made by the hon. member for Greenwood. I shall permit him to make that reply because I did not hear that part of the debate, and I believe it is the duty of the Chair to allow replies to be made.
May I, however, take a minute of the time of the committee to point out that we shall quite probably be debating these taxation resolutions for some time and that, if I may say so, whether we are under a socialist or any other form of government, we are faced at the moment with certain amendments to be made to the Income Tax Act. May I warn all hon. members that in so far as any of us introduce matters extraneous to the Income Tax Act we are going to provoke somebody else to reply, and the danger is we will be debating the merits and demerits of socialism or segregated schools instead of the merits or demerits of the proposed amendments to the Income Tax Act which have been submitted by the Minister of Finance.
As I said, I will permit the hon. member for Nanaimo to complete his statement which I interrupted, and I trust he will be able to do so briefly. Then I trust that he and members who follow him will be able to relate their remarks to the proposed amendments to the Income Tax Act.

I will take only a moment or two. As I said, I knew quite well the hon. member for Greenwood would throw the Hon. Patrick Gordon-Walker at me. I would hesitate, however, to classify him as the hon. member for Greenwood classifies him. I do not wish to be disrespectful to a man who was a member of Her Majesty's government in Great Britain, but he is not very highly regarded as a socialist. As to the other gentleman, Professor Joad, before he went to his final reward he moved, shall we say, into the ranks of the unsanctified, to follow the definition of the hon. member for Greenwood, and renounced his socialist views at the same time that he embraced some rather fundamental religious views. I do not think they can be regarded as spokesmen for the socialist idea.

I do not intend to go any further with that matter except for one point. The hon. member for Greenwood laid great stress on the necessity for personal incentive. I do wish that he and people like him would look at the Canada Year Book and discover the number of people in Canada who are in a position to benefit by personal incentives. If he would look at the make-up of the Canadian population he would find that nearly 80 per cent, as he himself suggested earlier, are working for someone else, and therefore any personal incentives that may be offered to them now, working for private enterprise, would still be there if they were working under any other industrial organization. I think the hon. member tends to confuse, as so many of his way of thinking do, the position of the very small, minute and rapidly decreasing minority-who are able in a modern industrial society to exercise free enterprise and operate businesses of their own-with the vast majority to whom this argument is simply not applicable at all.
Coming to the budget resolutions, Mr. Chairman, I want to deal for a few moments with some of the changes that are proposed. First of all I want to deal with the first proposal to reduce the income tax by 2 per cent right across the board. It seems to me this is a fair sample of the type of fiscal policy this government has been pursuing for some time. I have looked up the income brackets and the appropriate taxes for them and I find, for instance, that a married man with two children and with a gross income of $2,900 a year will save 36 cents under this new provision, but on the other hand if we go to the other end of the scale and take someone with a gross income of $42,800 and a taxable income of $40,000 we find that he will save $324.
I know, of course, that the argument in favour of such concessions is that they tend to encourage investment in Canadian enterprises and the development of our country, which is a very laudable purpose, but unfortunately the record shows that they do not have that effect. I have before me two documents prepared by the Department of Trade and Commerce. I find that in 1952 there was invested by Canadian private enterprise in business enterprises $4,130 million. This figure dropped to $4,108 million in 1954, and it is estimated that for 1955 it will be down to $3,874 million. As a matter of fact, in 1954 it went down to $3,835 million, belying the optimistic estimate of the department the previous year.
That would seem to indicate that all these concessions to people with large incomes in the hope that they will reinvest the money in

the further development of our country are quite fruitless. They are vain hopes, and it is not taking place. It is, of course, the decline in investment that has caused the unemployment troubles we have had in spite of the fact that public investment has increased to some extent, but evidently by the results not sufficiently.
This is not the only field, of course, in which the government is being quite tender. In one resolution there is a further provision for mining companies. I should like to deal for a few moments with the concessions that were already being made to mining companies, and the further concession being made in this resolution. There is of course a fairly plausible argument for granting depletion allowances because the owners of mines are working a diminishing asset. But I have never yet been able to see why depletion allowance should be permitted beyond the total of the investment made in the mine. I cannot, for instance, see why if I invest $100 in a mine and get my $100 back I have a right, at the expense of my fellow Canadians, to insist that from then on until the end of that mine I am still permitted to write off depletion allowance. That seems to me to be rather dubious justice. I suppose the argument is the same, to encourage these people to invest again in mining enterprises.
We have another provision which exempts them from income tax for the first three years of productive life. I would point this out, Mr. Chairman: If a mine is not making profits in the first three years of its productive life, and it is not likely to do so in many instances, there will be no corporate income tax to pay anyway; if, however, it is a profitable enterprise, for the life of me I cannot see why it should not pay its fair share of taxation as soon as it begins to make a profit. Again it is an attempt to provide funds, I suppose, for further investment by those who have that risk capital about which we hear so much.
As I pointed out, unfortunately Canadian capital does not seem to be very fond of taking risks. It cannot have been, otherwise we would not have had the $700 million of United States capital that was poured into this country causing some rather difficult financial and fiscal problems for us. Had Canadian capital been prepared to make these investments instead of seeking safe, sure existing investments, I doubt whether our United States friends would have found so much scope. But we go on hoping, of course, that if we leave plenty of money in the pockets of people who make plenty of money, they will invest it for us in the expansion of our industry.
Income Tax Act
In actual practice we find that what happens is that we have to rely on the people of the United States to do that. The only advancement we get is when the government does take the money off the people and invest it, in spite of the rather foolish way in which the government proceeds with some of its expenditures and investments. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that today the government should very carefully reconsider this whole basic proposition that the economy as a whole is going to benefit by leaving as much money as possible in the hands of those who will not need to spend it all, and assuming that they are going to make the sort of investments that have to be made in Canada. As 1 say, the record shows they do not make them.
We have, in the first place, no means of directing that investment to desirable ends, to the sort of place that it requires to be put. We have no means whatever of controlling the volume of the investment. We have no means of preventing that investment from being made outside Canada, as it all too often is when more alluring investment prospects show up abroad. 1 should like, therefore, to see the government seriously consider abandoning this whole taxing philosophy that is based on the assumption that these savings are going to be invested in a way desirable to the people of Canada. Many of the sections of this resolution appear to be based on that.
For instance, we have a special provision with regard to the cost of financial promotion. I suppose there are arguments to be made for that if you follow this basic governmental assumption. But I suggest the whole assumption has not been borne out by history. It has been proven to be fallacious. While the hon. member for Greenwood is optimistic that the system of investing funds which landed us in the soup once before, brought us quite close to the threshold again and is apparently getting us to the danger point now according to the figures on unemployment, is going to work this time, I would suggest the wiser thing to do would be to listen carefully to the voice of history and admit the unpleasant fact that this method of investing surplus wealth has not been able in the past to ensure the continuous expansion of our economy, and has not been able to ensure continuous employment for our people. Until we have some direction of investment in this country, we are always going to be liable to that disastrous decline in production and consumption which has accompanied private investment in the past years.

Income Tax Act

Could the minister explain just why item No. 5 is included here? I am assuming it means that rental income, after all expenses, depreciation and so on, is to be classified as earned income instead of unearned income. Why is the change made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I shall be glad to answer the question, but I wonder if, since we are going to have a question period at this time, we could dispose of the first four resolutions and then I could answer the fifth.

On resolution No. 5:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

We felt this would add some slight incentive, perhaps more than slight, to the person trying to retain or increase investment in rented real estate, by taking off the burden of the 4 per cent surtax. For that purpose, we are moving it into earned income.

I think it might even work the other way, Mr. Chairman. I know of several instances where real estate is held, and after depreciation is deducted there is actually a net loss. The real estate loss is deductible from other investment income, so I do not think it always works out that way.

On resolution No. 6:
What is the purpose of putting an investment company on a straight 20 per cent basis instead of allowing an election?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We have had a great many representations, Mr. Chairman, from investment companies that the present provision permitting election under certain terms is not wholly satisfactory because of the nature of their income, and claiming to be tax exempt in every respect. This is an effort to alter what has been unsatisfactory from the standpoint of the investment companies. So far as we are concerned we think that they have an argument in that respect. We have adopted a more understandable form of common taxation for all investment companies, placing them at the lowest taxation rate for corporations.
Is the minister saying investment companies have asked for this change?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I did not mean to convey that. They had asked for an alteration in the present law, and this alteration has been the one which we have devised. Whether

or not they are satisfied with it, I presume we will know after they have read the bill.

Will the minister explain exactly what their taxation position is at the moment, that is before this new legislation comes into effect? My understanding is that in those cases where their income was largely from shares, they largely escaped taxation. But they did have a right of election. Can the minister explain to us what the situation has been? How many of those who did elect escaped taxation, and for what reason? What is their rough position going to be now that they are all to be subject to taxation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: This is one of the most complicated and technical of the resolutions. Perhaps the hon. member would, therefore, permit me to read an explanation. Companies can qualify as investment companies if they meet the requirements of section 69 of the act. When the dividend tax credit for individuals was introduced a few years ago, shareholders of investment companies found they could not obtain this tax credit for dividend allowance. They were, however, able to elect to pay a tax. Investment companies have been considered as really just a funnel through which the investors, if they qualify-
Will the parliamentary assistant permit a question? If they elect-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Then the shareholders would have got the 20 per cent dividend allowance; but it was thought that it would be better to make them all pay and make them all entitled to the dividend credit.

Take the case of a company that had income, let us say, 95 per cent of which came from shares and 5 per cent from bonds. If they elected to pay, am I correct in understanding that they elected to pay so that the shareholders then would be entitled to claim 20 per cent?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is right.

As it stands now, they will pay, but of course pay only on their taxable income which would be their income from bonds, so that on the income that they get they would still be in a position to take the 20 per cent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: On the shares.
What is the final result of that? There is no longer any option. Am I correct in thinking the situation now is what it would have been before if everyone had elected to pay the tax?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
It is very small, Mr. Chairman. The estimate is that the revenues

would actually have a net loss of about $250,000 for the current year and in a full year about $400,000.

I want to go back to resolution No. 5 and resolution No. 10 together. In resolution No. 5 the minister sets out that:
. . . rental income from real property shall not be included in income to which the additional 4 per cent tax on investment income applies.
In resolution No. 10 it says:
. . . a corporation more than 10 per cent of whose gross revenue was derived from rents be disqualified from being treated for tax purposes as a non-resident-owned investment corporation.
Apparently the principle here is that of removing rental income from the investment category and placing it in the category of earned income. The minister, in presenting resolution No. 5, stated in part:
In the case of rental incomes derived from the ownership and management of real estate, it has been found impossible to draw a consistent line defining the "carrying on of a business".
This conclusion has apparently been applied in resolution No. 10 in disqualifying the investment feature. My question is this. Section 68 (1) (b) and (c) describe a personal corporation as one who:
. . . derives at least one-quarter of its income from . . , rents, . . . and did not carry on an active financial, commercial or industrial business.
Then the application of the principle involved in resolutions No. 5 and No. 10 would apparently remove from the classification of personal corporation a company more than 75 per cent of whose gross revenue was derived from rents, or sources other than those mentioned in subsection 1 (b). That is a complicated statement. I am wondering whether that is the intention?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I think it can be said that neither of these paragraphs, 5 and 10, interferes with or affects the present legal definition and status of a personal corporation.
I would say that paragraphs 5 and 10 are each also quite distinct. Paragraph 5 refers to a Canadian taxpayer who has rental income, and the change is being made because it has been very difficult to draw a line between what would be income from carrying on a business and providing management and not subject to surtax or rental income that in some cases would be considered investment income and subject to the surtax.
Paragraph 10, of course, applies to a nonresident investment corporation, which has been exempt from regular corporation taxes if they meet certain conditions in the definition. An individual who is a non-resident and is receiving rents from Canadian sources has two things open to him. One, he may be charged the 15 per cent withholding tax

Income Tax Act
on the gross rental that is paid to him as a non-resident, or he could file a business return statement and show his expenses and his income and pay the regular graduated personal tax on the net income. At present a non-resident-owned investment corporation can own real estate in Canada and pay tax at 15 per cent on only the net return from rentals after deducting expenses.

Where does that leave the personal corporation? Let me read the definition of it from section 68 of the Income Tax Act:
In this act, a "personal corporation" means a corporation that, during the whole of the taxation year in respect of which the expression is being applied,
(a)	was controlled, whether through holding a majority of the shares of the corporation or in any other manner whatsoever, by an individual resident in Canada, by such an individual and one or more members of his family who were resident in Canada or by any other person on his or their behalf:
(b)	derived at least one-quarter of its income from
(i) ownership of or trading or dealing in bonds, shares, debentures, mortgages, hypothecs, bills, notes or other similar property or an interest therein,
(if) lending money with or without securities,
(iii)	rents, hire of chattels, charterparty fees or remunerations, annuities, royalties, interest or dividends, or
(iv)	estates or trusts; and
(c)	did not carry on an active financial, commercial or industrial business.
My question is: Section 68 describes a personal corporation which derives at least one-quarter of its income from rents; has section 10 therefore removed from the classification of personal corporation a company more than 75 per cent of whose gross revenues were derived from rents, or sources other than those mentioned in subsection 1 (b)?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Paragraph 10 does not in any way affect the definition of a personal corporation because a personal corporation is defined in 68, and we are not disturbing that. Section 10 relates to a non-resident-owned investment corporation, and that is defined in section 70. I cannot see any relationship. I certainly will take my hon. friend's question as notice, and if there is anything I have missed I shall certainly give him a full explanation when we come to the statute.
While we are on resolution 10 may I ask a further question? Will the parliamentary assistant explain the reason for that change?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The reason is that this puts a non-resident-owned investment corporation in a fairer position with respect to a resident corporation. My hon. friend will also note that it is not suggested that the

Income Tax Act
change will come into effect in this taxation year. The non-resident corporations are thus given notice of our intention and they will have the opportunity-I think it is to the end of this year-to divest themselves of some rental income if it is consequential and so that they will get their rental income down below the 10 per cent if they want the low tax rate.
I am still not quite clear. Am I correct in understanding that this is designed to remove a situation which gives an unfair advantage to the non-resident-owned corporation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, the other way around.
As distinct from the domestic corporation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It will make fairer the position of the resident corporation who has rental income as against the non-resident investment corporation. The non-resident investment corporation has been able to escape regular rates of tax with respect to substantial rental income earned in Canada.
Then it is competition with the Canadian resident that is being considered. The non-resident has had an unfair advantage as against the Canadian resident?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes.
That is what you are doing away with?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Right.

Could the parliamentary assistant give us some further explanation in connection with resolution 13, because I am a little puzzled to understand the wording. Presumably this provision is intended for mines in the process of development.

speechtext: This is merely putting into regular statutory form what has been available for some time on a temporary basis and which was extended year by year. This makes the thing permanent until there is a change in the statute.
This gives the mining companies exemption for the first three years of production?

It is intended to permit a mine to get on its feet?

Before it becomes a paying proposition. Why is this necessary?

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance was tied up with the provincial ministers of finance when I discussed income tax problems during my budget speech on April 28. I am sure the minister has been too busy since then to refer to those remarks, but I should like to have the parliamentary assistant make some comment on the few figures I gave then.
I might say that I was one of the very few members of parliament who did not cheer the night of the budget address when the minister announced a reduction in income tax. I feel that those in Canada who are fortunate enough to be able to pay income tax should not complain about the burden of taxation. In spite of all that has been said I do not think that the present Canadian income tax schedule can be classified as interfering with incentive.
On April 28 I referred to a table which had been prepared on the basis of information as to the distribution of non-farm income in Canada. According to this analysis 34-2 per cent of all families in Canada are in the position where they receive less than $2,500 per year. Then next we find that 63-8 per cent have incomes ranging from $2,500 to $9,999, while about 2 per cent have incomes of over $10,000.

I am sure that it must come as quite a surprise to hon. members in this chamber, many of whom have had the privilege of having taxable incomes, to realize that only 2 per cent of the families in Canada receive over $10,000. When one considers the schedule provided by the minister in his budget he will realize that when you get up to $50,000, $100,000 and $200,000 in the way of interest the percentage would be very small.
Taxation statistics for 1954 indicate that there are only 330 persons in Canada receiving incomes of over $100,000. It is true that they receive a very sizeable total of $48.1 million. Then in the group between $50,000 and $100,000 there are 1,510 persons. There are only 1,840 persons in Canada who receive incomes of over $50,000, and together those two groups receive $143 million. That very small group really should not complain about the taxes they have to pay. As has been stated so often, it is not how much you pay that really matters, it is how much you have left.
As I mentioned when I spoke before, a person getting $100,000 a year would have to pay a sizeable amount but after paying his taxes he would have left, on the basis of 300 days in the year, $163 a day to spend. The person getting $200,000 a year would have left $261 a day, while the person getting $400,000 would have left $419.38 per day.
I submit in all seriousness that before we give substantial relief to the persons in those brackets we should try somehow or other to get more people into the brackets where they would be paying income tax. It has not always been considered to be one of the responsibilities of the Minister of Finance to be concerned about the distribution of the national income, but I think the real objective of income tax has been to try to re-allocate the national income so that in the case of those who have not it will be possible for the federal government to have the resources available for family allowances, old age pensions, health and other desirable services.
I submit that in the next few years the Minister of Finance is going to have to worry about 34-2 per cent of Canadian families who have an average income of $1,500 a year. Anyone who has to go out to find living quarters on a rental basis, to pay for groceries, books, health and other services, will realize that it is just impossible to give his family the standard of living that we Canadians think we should have on an income of $1,500.
I submit that one of our fundamental problems is that 34 [DOT] 2 per cent who have to balance their budgets on $1,500. They are in the position where they are going into debt at

a most alarming rate. I put figures on the record with regard to credit buying and the expansion of small loan companies which I think supports my claim that somehow or other we have to find ways and means to provide greater income for these 34-2 per cent. Those people should be able to get their hands on more money so they can buy the goods in Canadian stores and put more people to work. I hope that between now and next year when the minister is bringing down his budget he will take more from the privileged few in the higher brackets. I do not suggest for a moment that he take all the income from the 1,840 people in the higher brackets and that would solve all our financial problems, but those people who are in those higher brackets really cannot buy all the consumer goods that are piling up in our stores. I hope the minister will make some comment on the table I placed on the record at that time and the fact that such a large percentage of Canadian families have to get along on an average of $1,500 a year. This distribution of farm incomes points out that we have a large number of families of two persons or more, actually 8 per cent, who get less than $1,000. You have another large group, 7 per cent, getting between $1,000 and $1,499; and another 8 per cent between $1,500 and $1,999. Some ways and means have to be found of seeing that we change this very large percentage who are getting an average of $1,500.

All incorporation expenses?

Am I right in suggesting that the idea of this reduction is the same as I mentioned before, that it provides funds for further expansion in industry? Is that the basic purpose of it?

Income Tax Act
If I am right in that assumption, then it seems to me that it would be more effective in producing new enterprises in this country to raise the exemption rate from $20,000 further up the scale rather than to provide the extremely massive tax reductions to some of the very large corporations in this country. The devil can cite Scripture.

It is both inventory and

Their return has not yet

8. That for the year 1955 and subsequent taxation years proceeds of a sale or realization of inventory or accounts receivable of a taxpayer upon or after selling or ceasing to carry on a business . . .

Let us take the case of
Income Tax Act
a man who decides to incorporate his business and sells to the new company.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think that transaction would be better shown if we had the statute before us. I would suggest to my hon. friend that I do that when we have the actual words that are going to apply in the statute.

When we come to a study
of the statute I think we will be in a much better position if we have a better understanding now. I find these statutes difficult to understand when I get them, largely by reason of the highly technical wording which makes them more difficult to understand. Could we not have just a play-by-play account of what happens here so that we may know the exact transaction that is contemplated and the exact way in which it works out? speechtext: I apologizp for intervening, Mr. Chairman, but I think the hon. member for Greenwood is making light of his knowledge of this situation. This is an effort to provide taxation for the sale of accounts receivable and inventory by a person or corporation in the manner which has been heretofore adopted. However, in every change in the law, in the sense of spelling it out, one has to put in many things. In the bill there are a great many explanations.

Might I interject a question there? At this point would the minister tell us exactly what the evil is or what the gap in the legislation is which it is felt necessary to fill? What are the difficulties they have run into?

speechtext: There is no evil whatever in any legislation that we have before parliament.
It might have been passed so long ago that it was done by another party.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Even then I do not think I would apply that adjective. Actually, we are making sure that a person who sells his accounts receivable or his inventory should pay tax on the proceeds. As my hon. friend says, we have a situation where a business may be sold. It may be sold by incorporation and sale. The point is that at that time or subsequent to that time, the man will dispose of his accounts receivable and his inventory.

May I ask a question
there? If I understood the minister correctly, that disposition would be made after sale by the purchaser.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I was trying to combine the two into one. It may be that in the sale the accounts receivable would not have passed in ownership from the seller to the purchaser

On the other hand the inventory might very well have done so under those circumstances if there was a sale of a complete inventory. But let us suppose the situation where on a sale occurring you had everything pass, including accounts receivable and inventory. So far so good. You may, however, have a partial sale and after the initial sale you will have a sale of the accounts receivable. The purpose of this resolution and the consequent bill will be to tax in the hands of the vendor the proceeds from the sale of the accounts receivable or the remnants of inventory, whatever they may be. As my hon. friend will see, there is a provision as to the method of taxation, spreading it over the three-year average.

Why is that done, actually? I refer to spreading it over three years. If a man has $100,000 of inventory and he disposes of his business, why should not that inventory be taxed at the rate in that year? He has paid taxes in the previous years on his profit in those years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is quite true. But I do not think my hon. friend would suggest that we ought to tax this wholly in the one year received because he would undoubtedly pay at a higher rate than that which we now propose to charge under this provision.
I am just wondering why the three-year period was picked. Why not five years, as is done in averaging farmers' income, or something like that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: One must fix a time. Three years looks like a good average which will permit fair taxation for what should be paid. But if my hon. friend feels that it ought to be one year or two years or five years, perhaps he can make a better argument than I can make for three years.
I just wondered what the purpose of it was.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if this is what is in the minister's mind. Suppose a company has $1 million of inventory at the end of one particular year and shows a $1 million profit; then say at the end of the next year it has a $1 million inventory and shows $1 million profit. Then in the third year suppose they sell the business and they happen to get $2 million for their inventory. The profit would be commensurate with that on the previous year's operations and so on. Suppose they sold just at the end of the year. There would be $2 million profit on that

basis. But this provision would put all the $1 million extra inventory over the three years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes; because quite obviously the increased value has probably not occurred all in the one year. There has been a gradual build-up of profit in the inventory.
It is really a protection against somebody showing a deflated inventory which he eventually sells at an enhanced figure. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes. That is what occurs. But I prefer to put it on the other ground, namely that it is relief against high taxation if it were charged in the one year.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?
Carried.
I wonder whether the minister could give us an explanation of paragraph No. 9?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: This is' another loophole provision of a rather technical nature. My hon. friend would probably like an explanation.
This is not a defect in legislation, by any chance, is it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
No. We sometimes find that the act is deficient. This paragraph proposes a special tax of 15 per cent on corporations the control of which has been acquired by a non-resident corporation or a tax-exempt organization in Canada. The tax will be calculated with reference to the amount of designated surplus the corporation pays out by way of dividends to the non-resident corporation or to the tax-exempt organization. The general procedure for a company which has an accumulation of undistributed earnings is to distribute this surplus as dividends so that it becomes taxable in the hands of the individual shareholders, or the company may elect, under the appropriate provision of the Income Tax Act, to pay tax on it at 15 per cent so that it becomes what is called tax paid undistributed income. This of course may be capitalized under certain other provisions of the act well known to my hon. friend-section 105.
The present law also provides that if one Canadian company acquires control of another which has an undistributed surplus this undistributed surplus of the acquired company at the time control is acquired becomes a designated surplus as defined in section 28 (6) of the act. Dividends paid, therefore, out of the designated surplus to the company that has acquired control bear tax at the regular corporation income tax rates in the hands of the controlling company.

However, it was found that these taxes could be avoided if control of a company with undistributed income on hand was acquired by a non-resident corporation or a tax-exempt organization.
If control was acquired by a non-resident corporation it would then escape tax?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It did, yes.

And this says that a corporation resident in Canada which pays a dividend out of a designated surplus to a non-resident corporation exempt from tax will be subject to a tax of 15 per cent. You are putting yourself in the position of getting the same 15 per cent that you would get otherwise.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

No. I should like an
explanation of paragraph No. 11.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Because of the difficulty of ascertaining just where and how income is earned in the operating of ships and aircraft most companies have exempted such income from taxation. However, the earnings might be exempt in the foreign land and also exempt in Canada. This is another loophole provision. We are just trying to avoid having Canadian companies become a haven for escaping taxation anywhere with respect to operations of this kind.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?
No. Could we have an explanation of paragraph No. 12?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: This is new. It has been found that non-resident owners of certain timber reserves in Canada have been able to escape the normal tax that is payable on income of non-residents. I explained a little earlier how the non-resident would be subject to the withholding tax on his income from rents and so on. This provision will be similar. It is to make clear that on incomes from timber royalties a nonresident will pay the withholding tax.

You say "from timber royalties". The paragraph reads:
That payments made after April 5, 1955. to a non-resident, computed by reference to the amount of timber cut or taken from a timber limit in Canada be subject to the 15 per cent tax on income from Canada of non-residents.
That is the ordinary withholding tax. It refers to payments but that does not sound like income earned.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I referred to "timber royalties". That is a common phrase by
Income Tax Act
which we would describe that kind of income, income calculated by reference to the amount of timber cut, stumpage and so on.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

I want an explanation of paragraphs 14 and 15. In that regard I wish to refer to an editorial in the Montreal Gazette of May 9 which is based, I think, very largely on a statement made in the house by the hon. member for Calgary South with reference to the whole question of depreciation. The Gazette takes up the matter under the caption, "Handicapping Our Own." As hon. members know, the suggestion of the hon. member for Calgary South is that we are not giving a fair break to Canadian enterprisers. I am going to read briefly from the editorial in the Gazette and then I want to ask if we may be given an adequate statement showing us the approach of the government to this question of depreciation, because it seems to me one of very great importance. I shall read briefly from the editorial and then ask the minister or the parliamentary assistant to reply. It reads in part as follows:
The discrimination against the Canadian investor in Canada comes about from the different tax regulations in the two countries on the question of depletion. The importance of these differences was well set out last week in the House of Commons by Mr. Carl O. Nickle, member of parliament for Calgary South. Mr. Nickle drew attention to the fact that the depletion allowances in the United States are so much more generous that a United States company coming into Canada has a huge advantage over Canadian companies.
Depletion allowances are basically a recognition that a well or mine producing oil, gas, coal or any other mineral is a "wasting asset", strictly limited in the ultimate production it can yield. If the owner is to stay permanently in business, he must continuously explore for new wells or mines. Therefore an industry that must be seeking new reserves to prevent expiry incurs expenses that do not belong to a business that is not concerned with "a wasting asset".
This principle, to be sure, is recognized in both countries. The trouble is that it is recognized far more fully in the United States than it is in Canada. Here is the difference.
In Canada, for instance, operators of oil or gas wells are entitled to a depletion allowance amounting to 33J per cent of their profits. But they may claim such a depletion allowance only out of net profits, if any, after other taxes have been paid. And they can claim depletion allowance only after they have completed making all tax allowances for the expenses of exploration and development.
Under United States law, however, a company is permitted to make deductions for depletion before, not after, it has recovered the expenses of exploration and development. And these United States regulations apply whether the costs of exploration and development were incurred in the United States, Canada, or elsewhere. And. in addition, a company is permitted a choice of method in calculating depletion allowance, whichever may be the more to its advantage: either 27J per cent of gross production income, before other taxes: or 50 per cent of net income after other taxes.

Income Tax Act
How do these differences work out in practice? Mr. Nickle shows how severely they discourage Canadian development by Canadian investment. In the first place, the huge expenditures in recent years have far exceeded gross production income. Only one-tenth of the Canadian companies engaged in exploration are in the position of having net production income against which to apply depletion allowance. The actual benefit of depletion allowance to date has been only about 1 per cent of the spendings made to replace and increase proved reserves. Therefore the conditions under which the depletion allowance is possible under Canadian tax law are so severe as to be inaccessible to most Canadian oil and gas companies.
In the second place, it is often better, under the Canadian tax law. for a Canadian company to undertake no exploration for new replacement resources but just to exhaust those already proved. In other words, the law encourages Canadians to abandon or curtail exploration at the very time when it should be encouraged. And in the meantime, the United States tax law is encouraging United States companies to do what Canadian companies are discouraged from doing.
There is no need to follow extreme policies of "Canada for Canadians". But surely there is no need to place our own investors at a disadvantage when competing in Canada with investors of the United States.
Now, that explains the argument and the criticism which is made, and I should like to have an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Well, I am glad to know we are on the last item just before six o'clock. I would not want anything I say now to precipitate a long debate on this subject which I must say, with due respect, needs a great deal of consideration. I am prepared to make a short statement for the record. I had expected perhaps the hon. member for Calgary South would be here either now or when the bill is considered to deal with this particular point. If I do make a statement I would hope that he and others would consider it, and at a later time our views could be expressed at greater length. Perhaps the resolution could pass in the meantime, if that is agreeable to my hon. friend.

I do not want the minister to read it on the understanding we are necessarily going to pass this resolution before six o'clock. I would doubt if that is going to happen. I do not want the minister to be misled.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Since it is still the last resolution, may I ask the indulgence of the house to continue after six and pass it, unless there is a great deal more comment about this resolution than it appears there might be.
Could we wait until we hear what the minister has to say?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I did notice that the hon. member for Calgary South had made a rather lengthy and quite serious contribution to the debate some time ago on this particular point.

Of course, he is well qualified to speak about this particular business with which we are dealing. The fact I am not prepared to agree with his conclusion does not alter the fact his views are seriously considered on every occasion he presents them to the house. The whole burden of his speech seemed to be the same as that which was interpreted by the article the hon. member for Greenwood just read. It seemed to imply that foreign investment in Canada is given a better break than domestic investment. This is not so.
It is quite clear that companies operating in Canada, whether they be Canadian or foreign owned, are treated exactly the same by our laws. I think the hon. member for Calgary South would agree with that. It is true, however, that in the United States there are certain provisions with respect to depletion allowances which are slightly more generous than in our own country.

Would the minister permit a question? Would it not be fair to say the hon. member for Calgary South was basing his argument on the over-all position of a United States company, including its treatment in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes, I quite agree. But I should like to point out, sir, that when the Paley commission in the United States came to look into the whole pattern of tax laws, both in that country and in our own, they came to the conclusion that the United States tax law was slightly more generous-I emphasize the "slightly"-in its treatment of the oil industry and slightly less generous in its treatment of the mining industry than Canadian law. I am ready to concede there are certain technical provisions in the United States law which are more generous than our own, but it should be pointed out at the same time that at the present time our corporate rate will be 47 per cent whereas it remains at 52 per cent in the United States.
I am inclined to think my hon. friend has been working on a rather slim basis if he is trying to show that on the over-all competitive position there is a factor weighted against the Canadian oil and gas industry. It is always easy to point out, of course, the more favourable factors in other countries while overlooking the unfavourable factors in those other countries. After dealing with the international competitive aspects of taxation, the hon. member attempted to show that our method of allowing depletion operates to discourage exploration.
I must say I found that difficult to understand, just as I have found all other presentations that have been made to me by the

various interested groups difficult to understand. The argument, as I understand it, is that a company, alter having achieved substantial production, is to a large extent deprived of its depletion allowance if it continues to explore. I am not prepared to accept that conclusion, nor am I prepared to accept the illustration he gave in the course of his remarks earlier this session. Every dollar of expenditure on exploration frees a dollar of profit from tax. This is the essence of the deduction for exploration expenses. The depletion allowance, so-called, frees only one-third of the profit dollar from tax. It seems to me it is quite obvious that the company which undertakes to explore is not discouraged therefrom, having regard to the fact that if from further exploration greater production is secured and he receives his one-third exemption on the profits therefrom at that time. His immediate depletion allowance is postponed because he has already secured an exemption from the deduction of exploration expenses. I have never felt the argument the hon. member has made-I must say that this goes as well for those associations who approached me last fall in this connection-is doing justice to the oil industry and the problems it has to face.
I believe I have stated fairly generally the position. If my hon. friend wants to consider it in terms of dollars, of course it is obvious that under certain conditions a greater tax benefit will accrue to Canadian corporations if we follow the proposal made by the hon. member. This does not mean it should be granted. All of us can think of special arrangements which would result in lower taxation for corporations, but it is not conceded that if they do not get them their exploration activities should be curtailed.
There are several points about which I should like to ask the minister, not related especially to this last item.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We have gone through them all.

May I say that we have gone through them in a way, but we have ranged all over creation. We did not take them up, as I originally suggested, item by item. It seems to me fair that the hon. member for Eglinton, who has been kept at a committee meeting, should be allowed to make what comments he wishes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have no objection, except I thought the hon. member for Greenwood and the hon. member for Perth had been working through the resolution systematically and I thought they were representing their party.
50433-276i
Income Tax Act

These are individual points, Mr. Chairman, which I think are not related to any main argument. I do not intend to discuss them at length.
Regulation No. 1000, passed under the provisions of section 26 of the Income Tax Act, makes provision for exempting the income of nurses-in-training. It provides that for the purpose of the section income does not include income from employment as a nurse-in-training. This relates to the dependent of a taxpayer, the dependent being the nurse-in-training. I fully support the provisions of the regulation so far as they go, but I am wondering why a similar provision could not be made in other cases.
At the moment I am thinking of the case of the social-worker-in-training who, from the point of view of public policy, could well receive the same type of consideration as is accorded the nurse-in-training. Perhaps we should say rather their parents, on whom they are dependent, should receive the same consideration. I should like to bring that to the attention of the minister and ask him if he will not give consideration to an amendment to the regulation to include within the scope of the exemption the case I have mentioned of the social-worker-in-training, and put her on the same basis as the nurse-in-training.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am afraid I am slightly prejudiced on this particular point at the moment. We had not considered it in the light in which the hon. member for Eglinton has placed it, and I would be glad to do that. I think I know some of the difficulties which in previous years have rather restricted the class of persons and led eventually to the opening up to nurses-in-training. I must say that I am not too familiar with the principle on which the decisions are made. I shall certainly consider the case of the social-worker-in-training.
Before my hon. friend came in I made a special appeal to continue until these resolutions were disposed of.
I am ready to go on. Some one called it six o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall we continue?

There are two other points, Mr. Chairman. The first concerns the large number of taxpayers who, at the present time, by reason of deductions at the source, are obliged to file claims for refunds. It seems to me that consideration should now be given to some change in the provisions of the act so that the rate of deduction at the source shall not be so high that so many taxpayers will be required to file claims for refunds.

Income Tax Act
At the present time, as I understand it, more than half of those who filed returns for the calendar year 1954 will be eligible for refunds totalling $146,000,000. The figures I have before me indicate that in Ontario alone 2,010,000 taxpayers are expected to file returns and that refunds will be payable in about 1,040,000 cases. This is rather typical of the position across Canada.
The method of deduction at the source in the case of persons whose incomes consist of wages and salaries is well recognized. I remind the minister that the percentage of deduction was increased several years ago. At that time the point was raised as to whether the increase was not so great that many people would be obliged to file claims for refunds. Now we have arrived at a situation where the government is taking, by way of deductions at the source, money from more people who are entitled to refunds than those who will find themselves having some further payment to make at the end of the year. That is a situation that should not be allowed to continue. Taxpayers whose income is drawn from other sources are not in that position. The position is accepted that in their case they pay the balance which remains owing on April 30, after they have paid their quarterly instalments during the income year. For that reason, it seems to me the time has come when the percentage of deduction at the source should be eased somewhat so that so many taxpayers will not be required to make claims for refunds.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The fact that the numbers claiming refunds appear to be increasing, as my hon. friend has said, would be an indication perhaps that the percentage being deducted might have to be reviewed. The hon. member made reference to this in his speech on the budget. I am making inquiry, sir, and shall continue to do so.

The other point I should like to raise arises out of a Canadian Press dispatch of March 17. I presume this has already been drawn to the attention of the minister, but I raise it for his comment. The dispatch is datelined Kitchener, March 17, and reads as follows:
An income tax official last night described as "vicious" a section of the federal Income Tax Act which gives civil servants power to seize property without a prior court hearing.
H. R. McGrogan of the income tax department in Ottawa said that to his knowledge no other government department, person or corporation in Canada has such power.
He told a meeting of farmers that under the section, a department assessor can at any time make an assessment or re-assessment. Whether or not the taxpayer owes the money, he must pay it

to the Department of National Revenue within 45 days. If he does not, the department has the right to seize all his assets to satisfy the assessment, Mr. McGrogan said.
I do not think I know the official mentioned, and I cannot vouch for the accuracy of his description in all respects, but I would ask the minister to comment on this matter. I am sure it must have come to his attention before.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, this is the first time I have heard of it and without appearing to postpone the issue may I say that that also would be a matter of administration to which the Minister of National Revenue might make an answer. In the light of that, at the moment I am sure that I am aware of the practice and of the law which permits the seizure of documents and the like for the purpose of establishing assessments, if that is what my hon. friend is referring to. I think he will agree with me that such a power is necessary, though I admit that one does not want to have to exercise it unnecessarily.
If on the other hand he is referring to seizure of property for the purpose of satisfying a debt, then I shall be glad to look at the appropriate section, if it can be drawn to my attention.

The press dispatch refers to the latter case. The seizure of documents is not mentioned. The taking into custody of documents in the course of investigation is a well-recognized procedure in the act and is not mentioned in this dispatch. I take it that the official is referring to the provisions of the act permitting the department to enjoy extrajudicial rights in the matter of the seizure of property. I have in mind the use the department makes of its right to attach wages and salaries for arrears without any judicial finding on the subject and without those restraints that normally attach to the execution of judgments.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am informed that this arises after a certificate has been granted by the courts as to the amount owing and that, acting upon that certificate, certain seizures may be made. However, I am told by one of my officials here that the particular matter is known and I shall be glad to see that the whole details are given to my hon. friend. I am assured that it is in consequence of sections 119 and 120 of the act which do provide for seizure after certificate, and that the press report does not disclose the full story.

There is just one final point that I want to bring to the attention of

the minister. It is a matter that has been up here more than once. It has to do with the self-employed person's right to participate in a scheme of retirement benefits. The minister's predecessor turned this down and emphasized a good deal the mechanical difficulties. I am not taking the time of the committee now to go into it, but I do ask the minister to give this whatever consideration he can because it is obviously a matter which, if it can be arranged, is of vast importance to a very large number of serious citizens of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have read all of the past debates on this subject, and I have received many deputations and I have spent considerable time with my officials discussing it. I think I should only say it is true that my predecessor did emphasize the administrative difficulties and perhaps placed the onus on the public generally to find a way around these difficulties. But we have given consideration to it, and will continue to give consideration to it, having in mind that Mr. Abbott did place on the record some of the difficulties and at the same time suggested that while the principle was not precisely that which was placed before the house by those who were representing the arguments that there should be such a deduction, nevertheless we know that a great many people feel that something along this line should be done. With that in mind we shall continue to study the problem.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Resolution agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Do I understand we are to continue with the excise tax resolution at eight o'clock?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on a point of order. This may be the best time to announce the business for the rest of the evening. Should the excise tax resolution pass, it is not our intention to go on with the Customs Tariff changes but to go into supply and take the Department of Agriculture.

Mr. Chairman, it is undoubtedly a welcome occasion when a resolution under the heading of the Excise Tax Act proposes reduction in or repeal of excise taxes on certain commodities without at the same time proposing increases or new taxes. Therefore, as far as this resolution goes, I am sure it commends itself to the favour of the house.
However, in accepting the proposal for certain reductions and the repeal of certain taxes and before going too far in our enthusiasm it might be well to remind ourselves that it was this government which imposed the taxes which the committee is now asked to reduce or repeal.
There are several aspects of the resolution and of the excise and sales taxes broadly that I should like to comment upon briefly this evening. I suppose the leading feature of the proposal now under discussion is the proposed reduction in the excise tax on passenger automobiles from 15 to 10 per cent and the repeal of the excise tax on tires and tubes for automotive vehicles. The reduction in the excise tax on automobiles from 15 to 10 per cent is indeed welcome, but I should like to submit to the minister and to the committee that this tax is still too heavy.
This tax was applied in the first instance and presumably continues today as a luxury tax; it was introduced under that guise. In my submission it can no longer be defended as such. To a vast majority of the owners in Canada a motor car can no longer be regarded as a luxury, but in the light of modern conditions must be regarded as a necessity. However, our tax legislation takes no account whatever of that fact. The burden which this tax has placed upon the automotive industry in Canada, and indeed the acute way in which it has been making itself felt latterly, are well known to every hon. member of the house. We have on every hand

Excise Tax Act
evidence of the increasing state of disorganization in motor car sales right across Canada.
The automotive industry is a major employer of labour in Canada. Any reduction in the unfair load of taxes now borne by that industry is bound to reflect itself not only in a more equitable distribution of the burden of taxes but also in increased employment of Canadian workmen. While I do not propose to protract my comments on this subject I wish to emphasize that while this modest reduction in this tax is welcome it points to the necessity of a more resolute approach by the Minister of Finance and a more effective grappling with the problem and the realization of the need of further reductions or the removal of the tax which has become to an ever-increasing degree an unfair imposition.
The position in which many motor car dealers have found themselves since the minister introduced his budget resolutions is also worthy of note. I am sure that all hon. members have had representations made to them by motor car dealers concerning the position in which they find themselves as a result of the budget proposals, leaving them in so many cases with large inventories of motor cars on which they had already paid the 15 per cent excise tax. With the public expecting to receive immediately the benefits of the reduction announced by the minister, the dealers have been called upon to bear the full burden.
The attitude taken by the minister when this question was raised originally in the house was, I suppose, the traditional one. In effect the minister said that he could not consider making any adjustment either in regard to the effective date of his proposal or in the tax-paid position of motor cars held in stock by dealers. He seemed to imply that these were the same dealers who had derived some benefit in earlier years when the tax was being imposed or increased. It may be that when these taxes were imposed or increased in earlier years some people would derive benefit in so far as they had stocks on hand, but it is entirely unfair to assume that those same people are in business today in the same way and are now simply being called upon to part with the equivalent of some of the benefit that they received in earlier years in consequence of the introduction or increase of this tax. This is a very different situation.
The matter was raised later on May 18 when a question was put to the Minister of Finance on the orders of the day asking whether he was prepared to give further consideration to the matter. At that time the

Minister of Finance indicated in effect that he would consider the matter. It seems to me that the time has come when the Minister of Finance must make his position abundantly clear. If he had no intention of affording any measure of relief to these dealers who are in the position I have described, then I am afraid it was a cruel way in which the minister may have given them some hope of relief when on this recent occasion he intimated that he was giving consideration to their problem.
On the other hand, if the minister has given serious consideration to the matter and if he is going to afford any relief in this situation it is time that he announced what the government proposes in that respect. If there is to be any measure of tax relief in this regard it must be proposed now because otherwise the administrative difficulties in calculating any claim for tax refund are bound to multiply as the days pass. Therefore the matter calls for an immediate announcement on the part of the minister.
When the government is announcing a reduction in the excise tax it is easy enough to content ourselves with welcoming it, but I ask the house to observe the commodities upon which it is proposed that the tax be reduced. All of these are commodities upon which a reduction in the taxes is justified and indeed overdue. But let us remind ourselves at the same time, Mr. Chairman, that there is a long list of commodities more closely and intimately related to the necessities of life than any of those on the list before us now, upon which no reduction of indirect taxes is proposed by the government. Do hon. members of this house keep adequately in their minds and on their consciences the fact that this government goes on levying under the Excise Tax Act taxes upon the very necessities of life, upon our clothing, our boots and shoes and household furniture, certain prepared foods, and indeed on many drugs and medicines that are essential to those who require them?
I do not know how long this government thinks it can justify the continued imposition upon the Canadian people of a 10 per cent sales tax on commodities as essential as these to the average Canadian family. Think of it-the government deriving revenue by an imposition upon clothing, boots and shoes, household furniture, drugs and medicines. I hope that members of this house will in their might and in their indignation make it abundantly clear to this government and to the Minister of Finance that they will no longer tolerate heavy impositions of this kind that add so grievously to the cost of the necessities of life.

It is well that we should remind ourselves also that these taxes are levied at the manufacturer's or producer's level and, as everyone knows, as these goods pass from hand to hand, to the wholesaler, to the jobber, to the retailer, and finally to the consumer, they attract mark-ups. Concrete cases have been given to the house on similar occasions without number in the past, to demonstrate beyond all challenge or question that a tax that begins as a 10 per cent tax at the manufacturer's level will in most cases become a tax of 20 per cent or more when the goods are sold by the retailer to the consumer. The consumer, in the case of these indirect taxes, is never told what portion of the price he pays for goods goes to pay these taxes. They are hidden; and because they are hidden they are popular with a government that chooses to go on levying these taxes and avoiding as far as it can the wrath of the taxpaying public, by not letting the taxpaying public know what portion of the price is collected by the government in taxes.
A tax of that kind as applied to the type of commodity of which I am speaking is doubly iniquitous. It is bad enough that there should be taxes upon these basic necessities of life, but far worse that they should be applied in such a manner as to go on attracting mark-ups, mark-ups on mark-ups, and marks-ups on mark-ups on mark-ups, all at the expense of the consumer. That is another feature of this tax which in my submission this house can no longer tolerate. The government is not going to remove these taxes from the necessities of life, nor substitute a fairer system of collecting taxes than through the medium of indirect taxes in the way I have described, unless hon. members of this house, aroused and indignant, make that demand.
One could go further. Do we stop adequately to ponder upon the effects of these taxes as applied to purchases made by municipal governments or boards of education across Canada? It is a fact that there is no exemption in favour of municipal councils, school boards or boards of education; and the municipal taxpayer, already bearing a crushing burden of taxation under the present condition of unfair distribution of tax revenues as between the various levels of government, has his burden increased by reason of federal impositions on purchases made by his board of education, school board or municipal council.
This is no small matter. Many municipal councils and boards of education have made representations to the government about it in times past. The increasing gravity of
Excise Tax Act
the revenue position of the municipal governments is emphasized by the degree to which municipal governments and school boards are expressing themselves firmly on this subject. Many of them have passed more resolutions in recent times than ever before. I should like to read a resolution that was passed a few weeks ago by the municipal corporation of my own city of Toronto, conveyed in the following telegram from His Worship Mayor Nathan Phillips:
For years Canadian municipalities through Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities have sought to have supplies and materials purchased solely for municipal purposes exempted from federal sales tax in the same way as exemption now granted to provincial governments, their boards and commissions, as well as hospitals. Government indicated that such exemption too involved, notwithstanding that other governmental bodies and hospitals were exempted and similar exemption given on books, newsprint and other materials used in newspapers and magazines. Municipalities now bearing crippling financial burdens and exemption from sales tax would provide some measure of relief at comparatively little cost to federal treasury. Earnestly solicit your support of such exemption when budget before house for consideration.
Similar communications went to all the members from Toronto, and I am looking forward to hearing something said on this subject by Liberal members from Toronto constituencies. It is time indeed that they made their voices heard on this subject in this chamber and that they declared themselves on this important matter of federal taxes on purchases made by municipal governments and boards of education. It is grossly unfair that in the face of the burden being carried by these municipal bodies the federal government should be collecting taxes on purchases of goods made by them for their use, which means for the use of the municipal taxpayer.
There is one final matter upon which I should like to dwell briefly. It is also a matter of high importance. Surely the time has come when steps should be taken to exempt welfare and philanthropic organizations from the burden of sales tax on goods purchased by them for use in welfare work.
This matter has been raised in the House of Commons before. For my own part, I have raised it every year for a good many years past. It is becoming more urgent than ever for these worthy organizations. There is not one of them that is not faced with serious financial problems in meeting the growing demands made upon such organizations. There are abundant evidences that they are now more alive than ever before to the unfair burden that is cast upon them when the federal government taxes them on their purchases of goods for use in their beneficial work.

Excise Tax Act
Let it not be said that the administrative difficulties in the way are too great to be overcome. Adequate safeguards could be attached to the type of exemption for which I am pleading here tonight. Safeguards have been proposed by many of these organizations in their submissions to the government. There are four in particular which I have found in some of the communications on this subject submitted by such organizations. The four are as follows: First, that the social welfare organization in question should be certified by the Department of National Health and Welfare as a bona fide social welfare agency, organized and operated exclusively for charitable purposes, the proceeds of which are used in the public interest and not for the benefit of any special individual or group. The second is that they should be qualified as a charitable organization permitted to issue receipts for donations which exempt them from income tax. The third is that the organization should be incorporated as a non-profit organization for charitable purposes; and the fourth is that it undertake an annual audit of accounts by a chartered accountant. With those safeguards there need be no fear of administrative difficulties or of improprieties on the part of those seeking this needed exemption.
Mr. Chairman, these are but a few of the urgent problems which this budget, in relation to the Excise Tax Act, has ignored. It is deplorable that, in the face of urgent problems like these, the Minister of Finance has chosen to ignore not just one, but all of those that I have mentioned. It will remain for hon. members of the House of Commons to make known to the government in firm and resolute terms that they will no longer tolerate a continuation of its imposition of the burden of these indirect taxes in the cases that I have mentioned.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare is in the house.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: He is always here.

I think it is time that he should make his voice heard by his colleague the Minister of Finance in pleading for consideration for welfare organizations. The bulk of welfare work in Canada is not carried on by government departments. It is not carried on by the Department of National Health and Welfare or by the corresponding provincial departments. The bulk of welfare work in Canada today is carried on by organizations of the kind I have mentioned. Why then should they be handicapped by federal tax impositions?
