They are not asking for any favour. They are simply asking that the burden that has been unfairly placed upon them by the federal government should be

removed from them. I hope the committee will have the opportunity tonight of hearing from the Minister of National Health and Welfare some statement to indicate that, as far as he is concerned and as far as his department and its policy are concerned, they seek urgently at the hands of the Minister of Finance consideration for this problem and an early removal of a burden of taxation which cannot be justified.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure we will all agree with the hon. member for Eglinton that one of the most deplorable features of the sales tax is its cumulative effect in what he has described as markups on mark-ups on mark-ups. But it occurs to me that it is hardly fair to blame the government for this particular feature of the sales tax situation because the government, like my friend the hon. member for Eglinton, is firmly committed to the maintenance of what is humorously known as free enterprise. This cumulative sort of racketeering is merely one of the features of the capitalist system.
You should make that speech in Saskatchewan.

I should be delighted to do so. I should be delighted to come and make it in your riding.
I am more heartily still in support of the hon. member for Eglinton in his attitude with regard to this imposition of sales tax on municipal purchases. For the life of me I cannot think what argument can be brought forward in favour of it. I think it is a vicious principle that a senior government should impose taxation on a junior government. When one bears in mind the fact that many municipalities-and many municipalities in my part of the world suffer badly on this score-suffer from the effects of federal crown property within the limits of the municipality, with the consequent very deteriorating effects on municipal revenue, that consideration would seem to me to be an added argument for the abolition of the sales tax on all municipal purchases. It is a fantastic proposition that the taxpayers as municipal taxpayers are obliged to dig into their pockets to pay revenue to the federal government while at the same time being obliged to pay the ordinary federal taxes. I think that is something that should be made one of the items on the agenda of any provincial-federal conference that is to be held in the future; I refer to the removal of this quite irrational and quite unjust form of taxation.
I now want to deal with the items that we have before us in this resolution on the

Excise Tax Act. I can see that in the first two items there is a certain rationality. When the decision was made to reduce the tax on passenger automobiles, logically enough it followed that the tax on tires and tubes for automotive vehicles of all kinds should be repealed. There is a certain logic in that decision to exempt this particular class of commodity with perhaps foreseeable effects on the economy. There is also a certain logic in the first two items of the section headed No. 3 which reads: "That the sales tax on the following goods be repealed". I can see some logic in the decision to repeal the sales tax on materials to be used exclusively in the production of feeds for livestock. There is some sort of reason to that decision, namely that it will stimulate, I presume, that section of our economy. The same argument can be used for section (b), creosote oil and other wood preservatives when for use exclusively in the treatment of timber, poles or lumber. There again there is a reason, namely for the encouragement of more economical use of wood. But when we move on to (c), (d), (e), (f) and (g) we simply seem to sail into the wildest flights of irrationality. I am almost forced to the conclusion that whoever drew this up blindfolded himself, took a pin and stabbed it into a list, and wherever it hit decided that would be the thing that would be exempted. Why in the name of heaven do we decide to remove the sales tax on material to be used exclusively in the production of terrazzo flooring while on the other hand if you want a wooden floor or a cement floor you pay the sales tax? If you want a terrazzo floor then you are going to have the relief that this provision offers.
Then we have subsection (d) which refers to perforated bituminized fibre pipe for drainage purposes, not to exceed four inches in diameter. Why should four inch pipe . be exempted and six or eight inch pipe not be exempted? Why decide to exempt four inch pipe? Then we come to something that to me is quite utterly daft. Why pick out rims for kitchen sinks? Why not rims for bicycle wheels or rims for eyeglasses? Why not soap dishes or kitchen faucets? What is the rhyme or reason for this? Then we have floor tile. Floor tile is going to be exempt in addition to material used in the production of terrazzo flooring. Then we have wallpaper. Why is wallpaper selected?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Because paints and varnishes are exempt.
Why not roofing paper or any other type of paper-

Toilet paper.
Excise Tax Act

Somebody said "toilet paper"-or tar paper or cigarette paper, any kind of paper? Why select one thing? If you have selected wallpaper as a building material, then why do you not exempt all building materials and be done with it? If, on the other hand, you are exempting it as a wood pulp product, why do you not exempt all wood pulp products? Where is the rhyme or reason to this? It seems to me an example of complete irrationality.
In Saskatchewan the socialists not only tax building material but actually tax the building of hospitals.

We should be very glad to hear from the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek later, I am sure. Seriously, I should like an explanation from the government of these last five items that are to be exempted from sales tax in order to get some idea of what formula has been used in selecting one material and rejecting another. They are not grouped into any logical categories in the way that the first items in this list have been grouped into more or less logical categories.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If I may answer the hon. member for Nanaimo, first of all let us take terrazzo flooring. Instead of being inconsistent we are trying to be consistent, and I think I can show the hon. member that we are. Every item that goes into the construction of a terrazzo floor is exempt, so all material under the embracing term "terrazzo flooring" is being exempted. As to fibre pipe, hitherto we have had a restriction as to the length of the pipe. It was only exempt if it was under 12 inches in length. A new process in manufacturing has resulted in the development of longer pipe, and we are extending the exemption to be consistent.

It is not the
length you have referred to but the diameter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Up to now four inch pipe has been exempt only if it was not in excess of 12 inches in length, and now that limitation as to length is being eliminated. I suggest that is consistency and a broadening of the field in respect of a related type. So far as rims for kitchen sinks are concerned, rims are the only item mentioned in this particular change because the sink as a whole, if it does not have a metal rim, is exempt already. We are simply making sure that we are not going to exempt sinks and then tax rims simply because a few kitchen sinks are built in this manner. With respect to floor tile, because we already exempt hardwood floors, it seems consistent that in that competitive

Excise Tax Act
group all floor tiles should be exempt and not just certain floor materials. As far as wallpaper is concerned, wallpaper is being added here to be consistent. It is in the same competitive field as paints and varnishes for decorating rooms. Paints and varnishes are already exempt and it is felt that there should not be a tax on wallpaper, a competitive type of interior decorating material.

I have listened with interest to the parliamentary assistant's explanation, but it still seems to me that the much more logical thing to do would have been to decide on a blanket exemption for all materials used in the construction of dwellings instead of going at it piecemeal in this way, adding one material this year and next year presumably something else. There must be some purpose behind this, and presumably the purpose of all these exemptions is to enable dwellings to be built more easily and economically by the people of Canada. Therefore why not do a job on it and exempt all materials that are going to be used in the construction of dwellings?

Mr. Chairman, Social
Crediters will welcome these reductions as, I am sure, will all other members of the house and the people of the country. It is natural that people in the opposition should so do because they do not have the responsibility for raiding the money to take care of the difficulties which need to be looked after in the country.
I should like to associate myself almost word for word with the remarks of the hon. member for Eglinton. I thought his case was accurately and admirably put. I think every member of the house would say amen to his sentences if he were free to do so politically. Of course all members in the opposition are free to do so.
I should like to draw attention to one important matter which, in the interests of clarity of thinking in the house, is of vital importance. Within the last two days a prominent member of the Conservative party made a speech in which he termed as inflation all the increases in prices that have taken place since the end of world war II. I thought that was one of the crassest pieces of ignorance I have heard since I have been in the house. May I urge that the hon. member for Eglinton and all other members of the Conservative party get together and try to find out, if they possibly can, what inflation really means and then talk from now on as though they knew. To call inflation, increases in prices which are a direct result of government imposition of taxes and to insinuate that they have come about
[Mr. Benidickson.l
because of a surplus of money in circulation in Canada is simply to confuse the people of Canada beyond all possibility of accurate thinking whatsoever, and certainly to confuse the Conservative party and all who listen to them and even reflect subconsciously on what they say.
That was one matter I wanted to get up and say something about after the Leader of the Opposition finished his address the other night, but I thought I would hold my remarks until a more appropriate time. If there is any one word which we as a parliament and a country must get the definition of clearly it is inflation, if we are going to think our way at all through the maze of confusion, difficulty and anxiety which hangs over our future. Certainly inflation is not a rise in prices which results from government taxation, from a strike of employees to raise their wages or from the deliberate manipulation of the prices of commodities upward by a company that finds itself strong enough to do so, as was done in the spring of 1946 by the steel companies of Canada with the connivance of the government, thereby forcing up the cost of production of practically every commodity in the Dominion of Canada. Now, we have certain stupid Conservatives calling that inflation.
We consider the source from which all these remarks come.

I think people will do that. But unfortunately, there are some who still believe in the fairy name "Conservative", and while they are getting over their affliction they will be led astray.
There is one more matter I should like to speak about briefly. While the hon. member for Eglinton condemned the government for taxation on various commodities, and I agree with him completely, and implied undoubtedly that such taxes, for example, as those on goods used by the municipality and on books and other supplies required by educational authorities-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Books are exempt.

Perhaps the hon. member for Eglinton was slightly in error, but to the extent he was not in error I agree with him completely. There can be no doubt that there are taxes being levied upon goods and supplies required by educational authorities throughout the country, so in the main the hon. member's case was well taken. While he urged by implication that all these taxes should be removed, he offered no alternative. Since the opening of parliament this year

we have listened to Conservative after Conservative clamouring for a reduction of taxation, but they have never offered even a hint of a suggestion as to how revenue should be raised if that particular type of taxation were removed.
We want reductions.

The important thing is that responsible men and women, elected by the Canadian people, could, in this portentous year of 1955, be held accountable for being able to offer some sort of a suggestion as to how the country may raise the finances with which to discharge the responsibility which rests upon the government. If they have no alternative, they should at least have the decency to hold their peace concerning the matter.
Now then, what would the Conservatives do as an alternative in order to obtain the money? They should get off in a series of huddles, and finally get their huddles together and come to a decision as to what could be done. Social Crediters make no bones about offering the suggestions which they have to offer. We will see immature men like the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace, who the other night flippantly talked about funny money. I do not believe that if he had a six months' course he could tell the difference between funny money and not funny money. He spoke of funny money, thus showing a sort of detachment from reality, a detachment which I must confess no member of this house has any right to manifest.
We are faced with an unemployment problem, for example. These people have no jobs. We cannot afford to sit here and flippantly talk politics while they suffer and their numbers increase. The Social Crediters do not hesitate a minute to declare that in a country like Canada it is possible to create a great deal of money on the national credit, just as was done under the Finance Act of 1914, thereby providing a very substantial increase in the national revenue of Canada available for the discharge of all governmental responsibility. Up to the present time there has not been a member in this house for the last 10 years who has attempted to rise in his place and offer to show the fallacy of our contentions. All they do is use this silly little kiddish remark about funny money.
I maintain it is time, Mr. Chairman, that sort of irresponsibility on the part of members, even if they are members of the C.C.F. like the hon. member for Nanaimo or Conservatives like the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace or Liberals like the hon. member for Temiscouata, ceased. They are
Excise Tax Act
all expected to be responsible men and women when they get here. Now, we Social Crediters offer that as an alternative and I challenge anybody in the house who thinks he can get up and in a 20-minute speech or a speech of any other length show the fallacy of our position. The challenge will hold right from now on until somebody takes it up, and when he gets through I shall take him on. I must say I will not be the only member of the Social Credit group who will be quite ready and happy to do that little job.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I know that complaint has been raised time and again in this house concerning the effects of this drop in excise tax on automobiles. The hon. member for Eglinton reviewed the matter adequately, I believe, in a general sort of way. I think it is only fair I should tell the house something about the incidence of this manoeuvre in my constituency. I shall deal only with the city of Lethbridge. I am going to quote small passages from certain letters that have come to me showing how seriously this is going to hurt my constituency. I start with a letter from the United Service garage in Lethbridge, from which I read the following:
The loss to this firm is small compared to most of the dealers but the percentage is still the same whether large or small, makes just the same kind of a hole in our profits. Our actual loss on five cars in stock and in transit was $461.53.
That does not sound like very much money, but if the $461.53 cannot be made up there is another bankruptcy to be added to the bankruptcies in Canada. This is the sort of thing which I believe too few people in this country take seriously.
I quote further from the letter:
One of the above units has been held up through road bans for almost a month, but the tax has been paid and it is costing us finance charges until such time as it reaches us and is sold.
We will also take a loss on the used cars in stock because the price drops accordingly, but as this is an everyday occurrence we cannot complain other than to point it out as an added loss.
Now, if that kind of thing is multiplied by several times, then this whole matter is not quite so inconsequential as the Minister of National Revenue has endeavoured to imply.
I turn now to a letter from the Lethbridge Automobile Dealers Association, a letter written on April 19:
A local survey indicates that the Lethbridge dealers alone suffered a loss in excess of $14,000 on the new vehicles they had on hand at the time this reduction was made, and this does not take into consideration the loss they will have to absorb on the large stock of used cars they had in stock at this time . . .
Your co-operation and assistance in having this matter receive proper consideration and action will be greatly appreciated.
When it is borne in mind that in that particular area, and the area contributory to

Excise Tax Act
that city, the farmers have not been able to deliver any more than just so much of their grain, then if the payment which the farmers make to the garages is not large because of that fact it becomes more serious still.
I turn to a letter from the Alberta Automobile Dealers Association, dated April 11, from which I quote the following excerpts:
We do feel that in view of the fact there was no protection given on dealer inventories, this is an unfair burden beyond the capacity of the dealers to absorb.
These are solemn words, "beyond the capacity of the dealers to absorb". This is another excerpt:
We respectfully request that you will make a recommendation to the Minister of Finance and the cabinet that rebates be given on new units in dealers' hands as of midnight, April 5.
I turn now to another automobile company in my own constituency, Marquis Motors. I quote from their letter dated April 15:
We feel that some representation should be made to the- proper authorities to have a refund made to the dealer on the automobiles which the dealer was holding in his inventory on his new automobiles and on which the tax has been paid and was subsequently reduced. If this is not done, in a good many of cases, the dealer will be financially crippled or may find it necessary to go out of business.
I know what is involved. I sympathize with the Minister of National Revenue and with the Minister of Finance, but nevertheless there are a number of people who have fought their way through for 20 years, all the way through the depression, all the way through the war and all the way through the vicissitudes that developed during the outlandish rise in prices that took place after the war, and now they receive this blow! I ask the Minister of National Revenue to take another look at this matter.
It is not my purpose at the present time to say any more relating to this resolution. I am quite sure I shall find it necessary to make further observations at a later time.

I am
sure all hon. members welcome the tax reductions that were announced by the Minister of Finance. However, I join with the hon. member for Eglinton and the hon. member for Lethbridge in the representations they have made with respect to certain reductions in the excise tax on automobiles. I feel sure that automobile dealers from coast to coast have been adversely affected by the 5 per cent reduction in the tax.
While I am sure that everyone welcomes the reduction, the fact that it became effective on April 5 without the automobile dealers being able to save themselves from having heavy inventories has resulted in a heavy
[Mr. Blackmore.l
loss. There are in my own constituency situations similar to those outlined by the hon. member for Lethbridge. The dealers in my constituency are hard hit owing to the fact that up to the present time the minister has not seen fit to introduce any measure by which the automobile dealers could be recompensed for the tax which they have paid on the automobiles they had on hand at the time of the tax reduction. I know of one dealer who had 9 automobiles on consignment. His total tax bill will amount to $3,859. That includes the sales and excise tax that he has paid. He stands to lose a great deal of that unless the government see fit to introduce a measure which will permit the purchasers of these automobiles to obtain a rebate of the tax they have paid. Automobile associations across Canada have indicated that there are about 35,000 cars in the inventories of dealers. If one were to take the average reduction in tax as at $100 the total will amount to $3,500,000. This is the amount that the automobile dealers across the country will have to lose. Cars are in a different category from a lot of other goods which are held by dealers. There should not be any great difficulty in administering a policy which would correct this situation.
Like all other taxpayers, I welcome any tax reduction. I listened to some of the interruptions of the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek. I am always interested in his interjections and in what he has to say. I was also interested in what the hon. member for Lethbridge said. He thinks that he and his party have some method by which the people of Canada could have the services they want, and at the same time not pay taxes, or the government could get the money to finance the various programs. The hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek and I come from the same province. We do not say that our Saskatchewan government is without fault, but I can tell him that under the C.C.F. policy we could reduce taxes and at the same time give ourselves certain services. As long as any government wishes to maintain the capitalist system and permit all the remunerative and profitable enterprises to remain in the hands of private business, and at the same time take all the responsibility of giving our people services, in my opinion there is no way in which that can be done unless the people are ready to pay taxes.
In the province of Saskatchewan we have been successful with the few small crown corporations we have there. In a few years we have been able to give employment to over 4,400 people. In addition, we have paid into the consolidated revenue fund over $5 million profit. While that may be small

when compared with the national income and what could be done in some of our big projects such as our fertilizer industries, yet it is a step in the right direction.
While I welcome these reductions, I should like to point out to the government that, with respect to the reduction in tax on automobiles in the dealers' hands, because of the representations that have been made the government in all fairness should do something about it.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to prolong the debate on this particular subject of retail sales of automobiles; but I do wish to add my voice to what my colleague, the hon. member for Lethbridge, has said. I do not suppose I am in a different position from that of most hon. members in respect of having representations made by dealers in our own constituency. In fact, most of us from western Canada represent rural constituencies where there are a good many automobile dealers who might be regarded as more or less small dealers. These small dealers who have half a dozen cars consigned to them are suffering losses of anywhere from a few hundred dollars to $2,000 or $3,000. That may not sound much to the Minister of Finance who is accustomed to thinking in astronomical figures, but $500 to $1,000 or $2,000 or $3,000 is an awful lot of money to many a small dealer. As the hon. member for Lethbridge has said, for some of them it meant coming well-nigh to bankruptcy.
This situation is also accentuated by the fact that the cash position of farming communities in western Canada is bad. When the cash position of farming communities is bad it has an effect upon all other types of business, which means that generally speaking things in western Canada are not good. Since the prospects for the sale of cars are not as good as they might be, the effect of having cars on consignment becomes even more serious to the retail dealer.
I understood the Minister of Finance the other day to give some hope to the retail car dealers when he said that the matter was under consideration. I should like to ask the minister or his parliamentary assistant if that matter is still under consideration and if he can offer any hope to the retail automobile dealers. I do not think they should be left dangling in the air. As the previous speaker has said, the total loss throughout the country may be a couple of million dollars or so. If that represents the over-all picture it should not be very difficult for the government to compensate.
I urge the minister to do this. I think this is the proper time for the parliamentary
Excise Tax Act
assistant to state whether this matter is still under consideration and whether there is any hope for the retail automobile dealer in this regard.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in answer to the hon. member for Macleod, I confirm that the minister has been giving this matter continued consideration. Representations continue to be received, but this is a most difficult decision to make. Probably the final answer will be given by the minister after he brings down the bill.
While it is true that there is a relatively small number of units involved when you are dealing with a large and expensive product like an automobile and therefore it may be administratively possible to rebate the tax on this particular product, the hon. member for Eglinton was good enough to recognize that it is contrary to tradition to rebate a tax reduced by a budget.
If a rebate is given in connection with one product, even though it can be done administratively without too much inconvenience and if one is willing to forget the revenue, hon. members will understand how difficult it would be to follow this same pattern with practically any other product. There is no question in the world that if the traditional pattern were departed from in this instance it would be a precedent that would certainly be pointed to any time there was a budget change that affected inventories of goods upon which taxes had been paid.

Mr. Chairman, I am wondering when this question was raised recently why the minister did not deal with it then as definitely as his parliamentary assistant has dealt with it now. One can readily understand the argument which the parliamentary assistant has made. Undoubtedly a problem is created by the precedent which may be set up, but if the hon. gentleman will look at page 3881 of Hansard, of May 18 he will see that the Minister of Finance did not meet the question on that basis at all. May I read the passage from Hansard. It is as follows:

Mr. Speaker, I
should like to ask the Minister of Finance if he has received a brief from the motor car dealers' association of British Columbia asking for his consideration of their request for a refund of the excise taxes paid on cars in stock on April 5? Would the minister say whether he will be able to give further and favourable consideration to this admittedly difficult problem, and whether he is able to hold out any encouragement to that association?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I
received briefs not only from the British Columbia motor car dealers' association but from the national body. I think from all of the provincial bodies, and from quite a number of individual dealers.

Excise Tax Act
Of course we accept these representations along with all others and give them our best consideration.
Consideration is always welcome, but how about encouragement?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Encouragement is a word which I think is used on every occasion by this government as to its intentions with respect to the Canadian economy.
I repeat what I said when speaking earlier, that if the Minister of Finance had full knowledge of the difficulties which his parliamentary assistant has just outlined and if he meant to follow the traditional rule and not give any rebate on tax-paid cars as of the date of the budget, then he ought not to have made the statement which I have just read. If he did not mean to give any consideration to the matter, if he did not mean to entertain the request, then it seems to me that in all fairness and frankness he should have said so. Why did he not rise and point to the difficulties which the parliamentary assistant has just outlined? That would have been fair; that would have been frank. Those who had made the representations to the minister and to which the minister intimated he was going to give his best consideration would not have been misled, as I am sure many of them must have been, into thinking that there was some hope that they would receive remedial consideration at the hands of the Minister of Finance.
At the time the minister answered the questions asked by the hon. member for Kamloops I heard a remark made that if he did not mean to give some form of rebate to these dealers he should have said so then and there. It was nothing short of cruelty to buoy up their hopes by allowing them to think that their representations were being considered and there was a chance that some form of relief would be coming to them as a result of that consideration.
I think that there has been a lack of frankness in this matter. Whatever difficulties exist, as described by the parliamentary assistant, certainly did exist on May 18 and were fully known then to the Minister of Finance. If he did not mean to give consideration, if he did not mean to do anything for these dealers, then he owed it to them and owed it to this house to be frank in the answer he made to the question then put.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I said that the minister was giving this matter consideration and would give the final advice to the house when the bill comes up, probably early next week.
In the face of what the parliamentary assistant has said I would think that there was much room for consideration.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I just pointed out some of the obstacles.

Mr. Chairman, coming as I do from a city constituency it was natural that the automobile dealers there would approach me to make representations to the minister. However, other members of our party have done this and up to the moment I have not repeated those representations. However, there are one or two comments I should like to make.
I am not rising tonight because I was approached by these dealers; I rise because I feel that there is some injustice in this particular measure. I remember the last time when taxation was removed-I think it was 10 per cent on that occasion-a large dealer in our city told me, and I have no reason to doubt his word, that he lost some $7,000 at that particular time. I think they took some warning at that time and I must say in fairness that the dealers on this occasion, when 5 per cent of the remaining 15 per cent was removed, were careful not to be caught with large numbers of cars in their inventories, either in transit or at their selling place. They raised with me one point which I do not think has been discussed tonight, and I might ask the assistant to the minister for his opinion on that. They reported to me that this was actually a consumer's tax. It has been the consumer, the person who buys and drives a car, who has been paying this tax, and the government has been using the dealer simply as an instrument of collection. The dealers rather resent this. When the government has used them as tax collectors they find themselves in the position that, instead of the tax being passed on, as is usually the case, to the consumer, they are just a few men having to pay the tax which under ordinary circumstances would be spread over many. I should like a comment, perhaps from the minister's assistant, in that regard. Is it not actually a consumer's tax in that sense, that those dealers have actually no responsibility to pay it except the responsibility now put on them by the minister's decree?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, according to the language of the act, I believe it could be said that it is a tax on the manufacturer. It is at that level that the tax begins. As to what competitive conditions will cause in a business subject to a tax, we can each only form our own opinions. My hon. friend from Saskatoon referred, of course, to another drop in a tax that occurred in 1952, when the excise tax went down from 25 to 15 per cent. It is now going from 15 to 10 per cent.
I remind him that even since the end of the war there have been a few increases. What the trade did at that time, he knows as well as I do.

In any case, Mr. Chairman, I would point out to the minister, through Hamard. if he is not listening to me, that there has been a considerable protest in this house in regard to the matter, sufficient protest to make me think that there is at least a general interest. Whether that has been prompted by the fact that those who have suffered have made themselves particularly vocal, or whether they are like myself-and I have no doubt that is so in many cases-imbued with the idea that this is an unjust measure, we have had protests raised by members of every party in this house, including a good many members of the government party as well as those who sit on the opposition side. Tonight we have had protests from the Conservative, C.C.F. and Social Credit parties. I have not heard any of my Liberal friends speaking tonight, but I certainly did on a recent occasion when they were discussing the budget provisions generally after the minister had produced his budget in this house. I hope that the minister may still, at this late date, take the matter under advisement and perhaps reconsider his decision.

Mr. Chairman, I do not know that I want to deal with the question that has been occupying the attention of the committee, with respect to automobiles, but I should like to subscribe wholeheartedly to a point made by the hon. member for Eglinton. That is not, of course, when he referred to the imposition of sales tax, by implication, as if the party which is presently in government was the only one that subscribed to sales tax. For the moment it might be worth while to recall that taxation on sales was introduced in 1920, and at that time there was the most unusual situation in Canada that the Liberal party was not in the seat of government. Coming back to the point to which I should like to speak and on which I am in full sympathy and cooperation with the hon. member for Eglinton, it seems to me that, when a sales tax is imposed upon basic foods and almost all the items that are described as foods-and I specify only a few of them now such as milk, fruit, bread, butter, vegetables, rice, sugar, soups-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Is my hon. friend pointing out the things that are exempt or the things that are taxed? None of those things which he mentions are taxed-*

These are food products but, it seems to me, food products which are so common now as tea and coffee might also be subject to exemption. It may be that all these other items would be subject to exemption.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: They are.

But certainly an item such as tea or coffee, like an automobile, may perhaps be no longer regarded as a luxury but as a necessity in this modern day. I would suggest that consideration might well be given to bringing tea and coffee under the list of exemptions.

I wish to add just one word in regard to one point made by the hon. member for Eglinton-taxation on charitable institutions. That seems to me to stand in a class by itself. It has been pointed out that it does not really make sense to tax the other levels of government; we are just taking money from one pocket and putting it in the other. But when we come to the charitable institutions, it seems to me that they occupy a position different from everybody else. They are maintained by voluntary subscriptions of individuals, and they are doing work which cannot be done by other people. Whilst the parliamentary assistant might say, "We actually charge our sales tax to other departments of government", that does not matter so much; it may be just good clean fun. But when it comes to the charitable institutions, I submit that this is a case by itself. I just wish to add my voice to the appeal for consideration of this question.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

I would have hoped that the parliamentary assistant would have something to say tonight concerning what hon. members have said about the continued imposition of sales tax on purchases made by municipalities and school boards and the same form of imposition on goods purchased by charitable and philanthropic organizations for use in their welfare work, and about the continued imposition of the sales tax on clothing, boots and shoes, household furniture and certain prepared foods. Surely the parliamentary assistant has something to say on these matters.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows that these matters are always considered at each budget time, and in the light of revenues that can be forsaken and having regard to the things that the administrators of our statutes say that they can do safely and without undue expense in proportion to the benefits being extended, these are always reviewed. Most of the items referred to by my hon. friend were again considered this year. Something was said tonight about its being a vicious policy-I think that was the extreme phrase-for one government to impose taxation on a junior government. Of course, his

Excise Tax Act
reference was made particularly to the lowest levels of government, the municipalities and school boards. Our contact with those levels of government, of course, in much more removed than in the provinces. Some five or six of the provinces impose sales taxes of their own.
They are not hidden taxes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Very few if any of the provinces, in spite of the close relationship they have with these bodies, exempt even their so-called children in government from the sales taxes imposed in the provinces.

Mr. Chairman, two wrongs do not make a right. If some of the provinces have a sales tax and impose the sales tax on municipalities in respect of the purchase of goods by the municipalities, that is no justification for the federal government's doing it. We have this clear distinction drawn between sales tax imposed by the provincial government on the one hand and sales tax imposed by the federal government on the other. In the case of the federal government the tax is imposed at the manufacturers' or producers' level, it is hidden, and the consumer does not know what he is paying. In the case of the provincial sales' tax it is imposed, as it must be constitutionally, at the consumers' level and the consumer at least knows what the tax is that is being imposed upon him. But, Mr. Chairman, even if half a dozen provinces impose a sales tax on purchases made by municipalities, that is no justification whatever for the federal government's doing it.
With respect, Mr. Chairman, may I say that it seems to me that this committee is still left completely in the dark as to why the federal government has made no effort this year to bring remedy or relief in the cases that have been under discussion. We are left to guess whether it is a matter of policy on the part of the government to continue this tax or whether they see certain administrative difficulties involved, or whether it is for some other reason. We are given no clue in the very brief remarks that have just fallen from the lips of the parliamentary assistant. In matters as serious as this, Mr. Chairman, surely the House of Commons is entitled to something more informative than what we have heard tonight.
Here we have taxes on the basic necessities of life. When this question is raised as a serious issue in the House of Commons it receives what can be described as, at the very best, mere cavalier treatment at the hands of the government. No reason is given as to why the government ignores these pleas
IMr. Benidickson.]
and continues to impose these taxes upon the basic necessities of life. Only in the case of the plea for the repeal of the sales tax on purchases made by municipalities and school boards has the parliamentary assistant vouchsafed to the committee any form of explanation, and even then it is not an explanation. It is simply an attempt to justify this tax on the basis that some provinces do the same thing. To the minds of reasonable men, it seems to me that will be no justification at all.
We have yet to hear one word from the government by way of attempted justification of the continued imposition of the sales tax upon goods purchased by philanthropic and welfare organizations doing work in the field of philanthropy which is basic and essential to organized life in this country. Instead of helping them the federal government imposes handicaps and burdens upon these organizations which are trying to do their work for humanity in this country. I do not believe that there is in the House of Commons one member who, if he were asked privately if he could justify federal exactions or federal handicaps being placed upon philanthropic and welfare organizations, would in conscience attempt to do so. Then in this chamber, when we meet here as a House of Commons, how can hon. members sit back and condone the continued imposition of these burdens upon philanthropic and welfare organizations and at the very same time condone cavalier treatment of the problem on the part of the government? They do not even mention it. They think they can ignore it when the question is seriously raised in the House of Commons.
I hope, Mr. Chairman, that hon. members are not going to tolerate that kind of treatment of a serious problem at the hands of the government. We have not heard from the minister. He has left this resolution tonight in the hands of his parliamentary assistant. The parliamentary assistant owes to the committee the same serious consideration of matters of this kind as the minister would owe to the committee if he were present himself and were piloting through his resolution. I hope that hon. members are not going to tolerate the way in which this problem is being ignored and sidestepped on the part of the government tonight.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?
Carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

Agreed.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Applewhaite in the chair.
DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE Administration service-
1. Departmental administration (including advisory committee on agricultural services), $496,998.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Hon. members will recall that resolution No. 1 is to be found at page 4 of the book of main estimates, the details at page 83.

Mr. Chairman, when the minister made his statement last week the intention was that the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand would reply and present to the house and the country the feelings of the opposition as far as the estimates of the minister's department are concerned. It happens that the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand is at home today, and so I am in the position of being more or less of a pinch-hitter. Pinch-hitters are, of course, supposed to hit the ball and score, but I am not so certain that is going to be the case tonight. However, I welcome the opportunity to make a few observations with respect to agriculture in Canada. When the minister introduced his estimates he was as optimistic under the circumstances as he usually is, but regardless of the way the facts were presented by the minister it is pretty difficult to make the farmers back home believe that everything is all right.
It has been said that most of the reductions in agricultural income have been caused by the difficulties in marketing our wheat crop, but may I point out that, while a great deal has been said in the house and in the standing committee on agriculture in the last few
Supply-Agriculture
days about the west, I am amazed at how little is said about the problems of the eastern farmers. I suppose it is probably because of the conservatism of the Ontario members that we allow the western members to monopolize all the time and to create the impression that the problems of the Canadian west are the only problems that agriculture faces in this country. But such is not the case.
In most of Ontario last year harvesting conditions of the cash crops were difficult indeed, and there was a considerable amount of waste. Thousands of acres of crops were not harvested last fall. Some of them were harvested during the winter and some this spring, particularly last year's corn. But there was tremendous loss through wastage and depreciation in grades and quality. We in the east also suffered considerable losses, but I am going to say that we have taken them with better grace than the western farmers.

I do
not think that is called for. We appreciate your problems.
We never hear anything about them.
That is up to you. We try to co-operate with you.
I am presenting now the problems of the eastern farmers. We have heard about the problems of the western farmers for weeks and months.
We are listening. Go right ahead.

In the past few years agricultural producers' costs have risen while the prices of many of the products they sell have gone down and in some cases are still going down. I have before me the statement of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. In 1951 net farm income amounted to $2,154 million, but by 1954 it had decreased to $1,357 million, or nearly $800 million less in the hands of the farmers to spend. Is it any wonder, therefore, that in the last two years, particularly during the winter months and even later, there have been as many as 600,000 people unemployed? Until the farmers have more money in their pockets to spend there are going to be marketing problems in connection with many of the things that industry and labour produce.
Hon. members will recall that through the war years-I am going to reiterate it-our farmers were told that if they would sell to Great Britain at lesser prices then they would have a guaranteed market when the war was over. Ceiling prices were placed on agricultural products, and if some farmer was caught

Supply-Agriculture
selling a cabbage for five cents more than the ceiling price his name was blazoned in papers all over the country and he was regarded as more or less a traitor to his country. But our farmers were told in the same breath that by means of the price support act, with $200 million behind it, steps would be taken to see that they did not suffer losses when the war was over. Not many farmers are taking such statements today with the same grace as they did during the war years. We were all prepared to make sacrifices then but now, as far as agriculture is concerned, nobody is prepared to go very far in making such sacrifices.
Our farmers, having produced in abundance, now find themselves faced with surpluses and are being penalized because they have produced in abundance at a time when consumers the world over should probably be thankful that they have. I am not saying there are not dairy farmers in all the provinces, but in my opinion the dairy farmers in the east in particular have probably taken as great a beating as any branch of agriculture. We have the fact that 2j million pounds of cheese were imported into Canada when we had a surplus of cheese. Oils for the production of a substitute for butter are also coming into the country without duty. For years the farmers have heard it said that tariff protection was a good thing for our manufacturers and for the people employed in our industries, but apparently it is only a good thing for our manufacturing industries and not for our farmers. They have to compete in the markets of the world, and that is particularly the case today so far as the dairy industry of the country is concerned.
Very well said.

I wonder sometimes whether the farmers should complain bitterly in view of the fact that many of them voted for the government. Maybe they should blame themselves as much as the government. I hope they will think that over before the next election rolls around. But another issue will be brought up and they will be soft-soaped. But will it be successful? I doubt it.
I have before me a clipping from the Farmers' Advocate of February 26. The subheading of the article is "The Prosperity of Agriculture and of Industry are Interlocking", and the article reads in part as follows:
The reason given by our government for this move is that it is necessary to balance our trade with New Zealand which has been buying more from us than we have been buying from that country. In order to make up the deficiency in our purchases, we buy their cheese. The question that a lot of people are asking is, why was it

necessary to pick on cheese? Was there not some other commodity that could have been bought- something that we are not already loaded with? Could it be that the expected feeble squawks of the cheese producers would carry less weight at next election than would be the case were the pinch to have been applied elsewhere? Well, anyway, the dairy farmers in these parts are really hot under the collar.
I think that expresses quite plainly the feeling of the dairy industry across this country. I mentioned the drop in net farm income. In the past the minister has been quoting the gross income of farmers but the gross income of any industry or any business does not mean a great deal unless you know what the expenses are. In the year 1954 net farm income has been reduced by $453 million.
Some assurances have been given by members of the cabinet that further importations of cheese were not expected in the future. I am just going to point out that these assurances are not too reassuring. The farmers are taking them with a little grain of salt. They are not sure whether or not it is in the book. It seems to depend a lot on other factors apparently, such as who the government's friends may be.
Then, there is a policy which affects the westerner just as much as the easterner and that is the policy concerning freight assistance on feed grain. I am one of those who believe that subsidies are an evil, but because subsidies in the form of tariffs have been a part of our policy for many years, subsidies to agriculture in lieu of some tariff protection I would say are a good thing. What is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander, so I would say freight assistance on feed grain is probably one of the best subsidies this government has ever introduced. It allows the western producer of grain to sell his product to the farmer in the east who is in the poultry or dairy business. This enables these farmers to buy feed a little cheaper so that when they sell their products in competition with the world, in some years they can earn a living. At a time when net farm income is down $453 million it is difficult to understand why the government would decide to change this policy in so far as freight assistance on feed grain is concerned. I reiterate, I believe that it should have been incorporated as a permanent policy.
I have a question on the order paper which the Minister of Finance spoke about today, indicating that it was almost impossible to answer because of the dozens of items involved. I will give you an idea of what I had in mind. I am just going to take one product as an example, potatoes. Except for

about a period of six weeks, potatoes enter Canada duty free. When Canadian potatoes are sent to the United States there is a 37-5 cent per bushel duty on the first 3-5 million bushels, and over 3 [DOT] 5 million bushels the tariff jumps to 75 cents per bushel. Yet potatoes from the United States enter Canada duty free except for a period of six weeks.
To change the subject for a moment, may I say it is my considered opinion that the agricultural institute of Canada and the federal Department of Agriculture should be asked to assist the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources in working out a practical plan of soil and forest conservation. The problem of such a plan in the northern areas is far different from what it is in the agricultural areas, particularly in central and western Ontario. I believe that in my county of Middlesex only 3-5 per cent of' the land area is under forest. We are, therefore, suffering from soil erosion as a result of rains during the winter and spring months, and soil erosion by wind if there is a dry windy season. We are suffering also from a shortage of water in many farm areas during the summer season. In many areas the farmers are finding that the cities are encroaching upon the country areas; the residents are drilling deep wells and putting in pumps that are capable of pumping enormous amounts of water. As a result, farm wells that have served families with sufficient water for 100 years are going dry. In many cases the farmer has to either give up or spend up to $1,200 or $1,500 to drill a well. These city residents are stealing the water from under the farmers' land.
At the moment, not a great deal can be done about it. This presents a very serious situation. Then, too, we see some of the finest land in the world in the Niagara peninsula going out of the production of fruit, vegetables and canning crops and used in the development of cities and industrial sites. In my opinion that is a serious situation, although as I said a moment ago we do have farm crop surpluses at the moment.
There is another problem from which agriculture is suffering and that is the problem of education. The farmer, just like any other Canadian, wants to pay his fair share towards education. We are not educating acres, we are educating children, and yet the tax in the rural areas of Ontario is based on acreage in many cases. Many farmers say that every acre they own should have a university degree, yet neither they nor their children have such a degree. The costs are based on acres, and I think that is one of the things that should be surveyed. It is one of
Supply-Agriculture
the reasons for the request for federal aid to education. I realize, of course, that education is primarily a provincial problem.
Some years ago, I am not quite sure what year, the Ontario government set up a commission under the chairmanship of the minister of agriculture, the Hon. F. S. Thomas. I believe the commission made a complete survey of the province so far as services are concerned, and tabled a worth-while report. There was a meeting of the commission held at the University of Western Ontario, and as one of the invited guests I listened with considerable interest to the briefs and statements presented to that commission. At that time I suggested to the commission that ways and means should be found of providing water for the whole of western Ontario from the lake Huron area. Since that time the C.C.F. group in Ontario jumped on that bandwagon, and claimed it as their own. The premier of the province and many of the members from western Ontario have also claimed that as their own. I wish to point out that long before that time I had suggested that very idea to the commission that sat under the chairmanship of the Hon. F. S. Thomas. Since that time I have had the opportunity to discuss this with a high-ranking engineer in the city of London, and he has worked out two or three alternative plans that would and could supply water to the western Ontario area.
Not long ago I was talking to the hon. member for Essex South, and he described to me the problems of the cash crop growers in Essex and the need of water for irrigation from the lake Erie or the lake St. Clair area. These are things that, with the co-operation of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, the federal Department of Agriculture and the Canadian agricultural institute, could be worked out in a plan that would be of mutual benefit not only to Ontario farmers but to all Canadians. We hear about these projects in the west. For less money more people could be served right here in the thickly populated area of western Ontario.
Yesterday it was my privilege and the privilege of the hon. member for London to join with 275 of the leading businessmen from the city of London in a visit to this House of Commons and to the Ottawa district. They are all conscious of the conservation and water-supply problem. We read in the press of the needs of the county of Waterloo. They are so short of water that they hesitate to encourage new industries to come to the cities of Waterloo and Kitchener. Therefore, they are facing a very difficult problem.

Supply-Agriculture
I hold in my hand the policy declarations of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce as they relate to agriculture. I find the following:
Seventeen per cent of Canada's population live on farms. These people not only constitute about one-sixth of the domestic market for all the various goods and services produced by Canadian workers in every type of occupation but are also the source of food and other farm products for the rapidly increasing urban populations. Food industries, which are wholly dependent upon farm production, rank among the 15 largest of all industries.
Farther on in the article they say:
Loss of soil fertility and erosion by wind and water are among the most important problems facing agriculture in Canada.
The Canadian Chamber of Commerce are to be complimented on their fundamental interest in the basic industry of this country.
It is a minute to ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman, and I think we had better call it ten o'clock.
